A file opens in **File** view, at its line: on **Working changes** when it has uncommitted changes, and on **Files** otherwise. A folder opens on **Files**, with its changed files stacked.

### Update many worktrees at once

To bring several worktrees and local branches up to date with their bases in one pass, use **Update** in **Settings → Repositories → Worktrees and branches**. The **Update worktrees** panel checks each one and lists what it will update and what it skips, such as a worktree with uncommitted changes, one where an agent is working, or a branch already checked out in a worktree. A local branch with no worktree is updated in place, without being checked out.

Keep each repository's default way to update and push, or choose another for this update. **Push + Publish** also publishes branches that have no remote branch yet. Nothing changes until you press **Update**, and **Roll back** undoes a worktree's update. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#update-worktrees).

***

## Opening a pull request

The agent can open the pull request, or you can open it yourself:

- Run a command in the worktree's terminal, or use your host's website.
- For a GitHub.com repository, click **Create pull request** above the **Todo** list. See [Create and manage GitHub pull requests](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#create-and-manage-github-pull-requests).

Once the pull request exists, Kepler tracks it as a task resource. A pull request gets attached to the task in one of 3 ways:

| Path | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The agent publishes it** | When an agent publishes a pull request on one of the worktree's remotes, Kepler attaches it to the task. You do not need to do anything |
| **The agent attaches it** | Agents can attach and detach the task's links themselves, including a link you attached. Kepler shows each one as a pull request, an issue, or a plain link, with its title and status where it can |
| **You attach an existing one** | **Manage resources**, at the bottom of the task's context panel, opens the **Resources** screen. On its **Pull requests** tab, tick the pull request, then click **Save changes** |

Only the task's own pull request is attached, not every link the agent reads along the way. Anything the agent attaches shows up in the task right away.

Attaching a pull request also unlocks the **Address Feedback** Action on that task. See [Actions](/kepler/actions) and [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations).

***

## Agent tools: AI Sync and AI Compose

AI Sync and AI Compose give agents Git tools they do not otherwise have. Both are off until you turn them on. Turn them on in **Settings → Agent tools → Built-in tools**. With a tool turned on, the agents in your sessions gain the matching tools, and you ask for the work in the chat. AI Sync also powers the Sync view's **Sync** button when the branch has conflicts. See [Resolve update conflicts with AI](#resolve-update-conflicts-with-ai).

| Tool | How an agent uses it |
|---|---|
| **AI Sync** | Rebases or merges the branch onto its base and resolves conflicts, with a result you can read before it applies, and every run backed up. It can push the result, and follows the repository's update and push settings unless you ask otherwise |
| **AI Compose** | Plans the new commits for you to read before it applies them, can split a branch into a stack, and can undo what it applied |

When you ask for a sync, tell the agent what matters, such as which side is authoritative, and it uses that when it resolves conflicts.

A running session keeps the tools it started with. To use a tool you just turned on, start a new session.

Both sets of tools work on the session's own worktree by default. Each can also name another worktree attached to the same task, so one session can clean up a branch it is not working in.

***

---
# Dictation and Read Aloud
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/voice-input/
product: Kepler
feature: Voice
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler has 2 voice features, both set up in **Settings → Voice**:

- **Dictation** adds a microphone to the agent prompt and to a Terminal session's status bar, so you can talk instead of typing. **Transcription runs on your device**, using a model Kepler downloads once. Kepler never uploads your audio.
- **Read aloud** reads an agent's replies to you. See [Read aloud](#read-aloud).

Dictation has 3 transcription engines:

- **Qwen3-ASR** reads what you're writing, so it gets developer terms such as Jira, rebase, or pull request right more often than Whisper. It needs a graphics card with WebGPU.
- **Parakeet** is fast, and understands English and 24 other European languages. It needs a graphics card with WebGPU and 16-bit float shader support.
- **Whisper** works on any machine. Use it where WebGPU is unavailable.

Dictation turns on once you download a model in **Settings → Voice**. The microphone in the prompt becomes available when the model is ready.

***

## Choose what happens when you stop talking

To record, click **Dictate** in the prompt, or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + Space** (**Toggle dictation**), and speak. Click the microphone again to stop, or press the shortcut again. The shortcut works in whichever message box has focus and a microphone, including the **New task** composer and a Terminal session.

While you dictate, the **Search Kepler** field in the top bar shows **Listening…** and your words. Click it to stop.

To change the **Speech model**, **Dictation mode**, or **Dictation language** without opening Settings, right-click the microphone. **Voice settings…** opens **Settings → Voice**.

To choose what Kepler does with what you say, go to **Settings → Voice → Dictation mode** and pick one of these options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Type as you talk** | Each phrase appears in the prompt when you pause, until you press the mic again. This is the default |
| **Type when you stop** | Everything you said appears in the prompt when you press the mic again, ready to edit |
| **Send when you stop** | The prompt is sent with what you said when you press the mic again |

With Qwen3-ASR or Parakeet, the phrase you are saying shows in the prompt as you speak. With Qwen3-ASR, **Type as you talk** can correct earlier words in a paragraph as you keep talking. Once you edit that text, Kepler adds only new words and never overwrites what you typed.

Kepler treats short, whole utterances as commands rather than dictation: saying "send", "cancel", or "clear" acts on the prompt instead of adding text to it. Kepler dictates anything longer verbatim.

While a transcription is in progress, the microphone shows **Transcribing…**. If transcription falls behind, Kepler pauses the microphone until it catches up. If this happens often, pick a smaller model.

### Dictate in a Terminal session

In a Terminal session, the microphone sits on the status bar while Kepler's message box is hidden. Click it, or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + Space**, and speak. A caption shows **Listening…** and then your words, and Kepler types the text into the agent's own input, following your **Dictation mode**.

Dictation only adds to the agent's input, so saying "clear" does not erase it: clear it in the terminal. If the agent cannot take input yet, Kepler moves the dictated text to the message box.

Right-click the status-bar microphone for the same dictation menu as in the prompt.

### Teach dictation your words

Qwen3-ASR learns how you spell words it gets wrong. When you fix a single dictated word in the prompt before you send it, Kepler notes the fix. After you make the same fix in 2 sends, a notice suggests the word, and **Review** opens the **Vocabulary** page. Dictation uses a suggested word only after you approve it.

**Vocabulary**, in **Settings → Voice**, shows how many words dictation knows. Click **Manage** to open the **Vocabulary** page. **Manage** works only while a Qwen3-ASR model dictates. On the page:

- **Suggested words** each show what Qwen3-ASR heard, with **Approve** and **Dismiss**. A dismissed fix is never suggested again.
- Below them, the words you approved and the words you added each have a remove button. To add a word yourself, type it in **Add a word** and click **Add**.
- **Forget learned words…** removes every learned, suggested, and added word on this device.

Kepler stores only the words, on this device only, and keeps them after you sign out.

***

## Set up dictation in Settings

**Settings → Voice** opens with **Check your setup**, where you can try dictation and read aloud before you talk to an agent:

- **Microphone** picks the microphone dictation listens to, saved for this window. Click **Try dictation**, the microphone button beside it, and speak to test it. Nothing you say there is sent to an agent.
- **Speaker** picks the speaker Kokoro reads replies on. System voices always play on the system default. Click **Play a reply**, the play button beside it, to hear a sample.

If the microphone or speaker you picked is not connected, Kepler tells you and uses the system default.

Below it, the **Dictation** section's **Speech model** list offers these models. Every model runs on this computer, and nothing you say leaves it.

| Model | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Qwen3-ASR** | Gets developer terms and mixed languages right more often than Whisper. Pick a **Qwen3-ASR size**: **1.7B** is the most accurate, **0.6B** suits graphics cards with less memory |
| **Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3** | A fast model for English and 24 other European languages that detects which one you speak. Listed only when the graphics card supports it |
| **Whisper** | Works on any machine, including without a compatible graphics card. Less accurate with technical terms |

Kepler marks the model that suits this computer and your languages **Recommended**. Without WebGPU, only Whisper can run.

To set up dictation, follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Voice**.
2. For Qwen3-ASR, pick a **Qwen3-ASR size**. For Whisper, pick a quality from **Fast** to **Most accurate**. **Automatic** uses the quality Kepler suggests for this machine.
3. Click **Download** on the model's row.

Your first download turns dictation on. Downloads keep going if you leave the page, and Kepler notifies you when the model is ready. With more than 1 model downloaded, pick the one dictation uses.

Once a model is downloaded, these settings apply:

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Remove…** | On a downloaded model's row: deletes the model and frees its storage. Removing the model that dictates turns the microphone off until you pick another |
| **Dictation language** | With a Qwen3-ASR model: the language you speak. See [Dictation language](#dictation-language) |
| **Dictation mode** | Chooses what happens to what you say. See [Choose what happens when you stop talking](#choose-what-happens-when-you-stop-talking) |
| **Vocabulary** | With a Qwen3-ASR model: the words dictation learned from your fixes. See [Teach dictation your words](#teach-dictation-your-words) |

### Dictation language

With Qwen3-ASR, **Dictation language** is **Auto-detect** by default, or 1 of 30 languages, each listed by its own name. Choose a language to always dictate in it. Parakeet and Whisper detect the language you speak, so the setting is unavailable with them.

### Model updates

When a newer version of a Qwen3-ASR model ships, a notice offers **Update**, and the model's row in **Settings → Voice** keeps offering **Update**. Dictation keeps using the installed model until you update.

### Linux graphics cards

On Linux, Kepler turns WebGPU on so Qwen3-ASR can use the graphics card:

- Under Wayland, WebGPU is on by default.
- Under X11, start Kepler with `--enable-linux-webgpu` to turn it on.
- Start Kepler with `--disable-linux-webgpu` to turn it off.

If Kepler's first window hangs or never draws with WebGPU on, Kepler turns WebGPU off for later launches and restarts. Without WebGPU, use Whisper.

For every dictation and read aloud setting, see [Voice settings](/kepler/settings-app#voice).

***

## Why the microphone is unavailable

Hover the microphone, and its tooltip explains why. When the model cannot dictate, clicking the microphone opens the dictation menu, where you can download or choose another model.

| Tooltip | What it means |
|---|---|
| *Download a model first* | No model is downloaded yet |
| *Dictation requires a secure (https) connection* | You're using Kepler over plain HTTP, where the browser will not grant microphone access |
| *Dictation is not supported in this environment* | This build or browser cannot run it |
| *Choose Whisper here. The selected model needs WebGPU, which is not available.* | A Qwen3-ASR or Parakeet model is selected, but this computer or browser has no WebGPU |
| *The graphics card is not responding, so dictation cannot start. Open Settings to check it again.* | The graphics card did not answer |
| *Loading voice model…* / *Transcribing…* | Busy. The button is disabled for the moment |

When dictation fails, Kepler names the cause, with **Open Settings** where Settings can fix it. For example:

- *A voice model is being installed. Try again when it finishes.*
- *The voice model is no longer downloaded on this computer. Download it again in Settings.*
- *The voice engine stopped responding. Try again; the model reloads on its own.*
- *Dictation stopped unexpectedly.*

***

## Microphone permission on macOS

macOS asks for microphone access the first time you record.

If access is denied or restricted, turn it on in **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone**, if your device policy allows it. **Open System Settings**, in Kepler's message, takes you straight to that pane. You may need to restart Kepler for the change to take effect.

***

## Read aloud

Read aloud speaks an agent's replies to you. Kepler reads only the prose: code blocks, diffs, and tables become a short summary. In the chat, the sentence being read is highlighted.

To have a reply read aloud, use one of these controls:

- **Read aloud**, the speaker button under each chat reply. While that reply plays, the button pauses and resumes it, and **Stop reading** appears beside it.
- **Continuous reading**, the headphones button in the composer and on a Terminal session's status bar. It reads the latest reply, then each new one as it arrives, until you stop. Right-click it to change the **Speech model**, **Voice**, or **Speed**, or to open **Voice settings…**.
- **Read aloud from here**, in the right-click menu of a message or a terminal session. Kepler reads from the sentence under the pointer through the replies after it.
- **Read the last reply aloud, or pause and resume it**, a shortcut for the focused session, with no default key. Assign one in **Settings → Keyboard shortcuts**.

During continuous reading, the **Read aloud** bar above the composer shows the sentence being read, with buttons to pause, skip to the next reply, or stop, and a **Continuous reading** toggle.

While anything is being read, the **Search Kepler** field in the top bar shows **Reading aloud** and the sentence. Click it to stop reading.

The read aloud controls appear only on a computer with a voice to read with. Read aloud starts with your system's voices. To change the voice, follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Voice**, and go to **Read aloud**.
2. Under **Speech model**, choose **System** or **Kokoro**. Kokoro has natural English voices and needs a graphics card with WebGPU. Click **Download** to get it. Until Kokoro is downloaded, and for text that is not English, the system voice reads. To pick the speaker Kokoro plays on, use **Speaker** in [Check your setup](#set-up-dictation-in-settings).
3. Pick a **Voice**. Choosing one plays a short sample.
4. Set the **Speed**.

***

## Remote windows

Dictation works in a window attached to a remote environment. The agent runs on the remote machine; the microphone and the transcription stay local, on the computer in front of you.

Over a plain HTTP connection the microphone is unavailable. See [Why the microphone is unavailable](#why-the-microphone-is-unavailable).

Voice settings belong to each computer:

- Every desktop window uses this computer's voice settings, including a window connected to a remote.
- A Remote Access browser uses the settings of the Kepler it's connected to.
- Neither the settings nor the models sync between devices.

A remote window or a Remote Access browser may need to download the model once. A different browser, device, or private window downloads it again.

Vocabulary words and the languages this device has dictated in stay on the device in front of you, and never go to the remote machine.

See [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments).

---

---
# Move from Conductor to Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-move-from-conductor/
product: Kepler
feature: Tasks
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken imports your Conductor workspaces on a Mac as tasks, in the same folders and branches, with their Claude Code or Codex chats ready to continue. You pick the workspaces to bring over in **Import from another app**, and Kepler leaves your files and branches where they are.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Bringing the workspaces the Conductor app keeps on your Mac into Kepler as tasks
- Prerequisite: Conductor's workspaces on the Mac that runs Kepler
- Limits: Importing from Conductor works on macOS only, because Conductor runs only on macOS.
- Limits: Conductor's cloud workspaces are not imported. They have no folder on your Mac.
- Limits: Archived workspaces, and workspaces whose folder no longer exists, are not imported.
- Limits: Continue each chat in 1 app only. Conductor and Kepler write to the same chat history.

***

## Quick Start

1. On an empty **Tasks** list, click the import card, such as **Import from Conductor**. You can also choose **File → Import from Another App…**.
2. If Kepler found more than 1 app, click **Conductor**.
3. Tick the workspaces you want, and click **Import *N* workspaces**. Workspaces active in the last 30 days arrive ticked.
4. The import runs in the background. When the title bar chip reads **Imported *N***, click it, then click **View tasks**.
5. Open a new task in **Tasks** to pick its chat up where it left off.

After you install Kepler, the guided start also offers to import Conductor's workspaces when it finds them. See [Getting Started with Kepler](/kepler/kepler-getting-started).

***

## How to import your Conductor workspaces

1. On an empty **Tasks** list, click the import card. It names the apps Kepler found, such as **Import from Conductor, Orca and 2 more**. You can also choose **File → Import from Another App…** at any time.

    
2. If Kepler found more than 1 app, click **Conductor** in **Import from another app**.

    
3. In **Import from Conductor**, tick the workspaces you want, and click **Import *N* workspaces**. The workspaces are grouped by repository. Workspaces active in the last 30 days arrive ticked, and older ones are folded under **Older**. To tick a whole repository, use its tick box. To narrow a long list, type in **Filter workspaces**. A workspace you already imported is marked **Already a task:** and the task's name.

4. The dialog closes and the import runs in the background. A chip in the title bar shows its progress, such as **Importing 2 of 4**. To end the import early, hover over or click the chip and click **Stop** on its card. When the chip reads **Imported *N***, click **View tasks** on its card, or **Dismiss** to clear the chip.

5. Find the new tasks in **Tasks**.

    
If Conductor is not in the list, Kepler did not find Conductor's workspaces on this Mac.

***

## What carries over from Conductor

| From Conductor | In Kepler |
|---|---|
| A workspace | A task, named after the workspace |
| The workspace's folder | The task's worktree, or the repository folder for a workspace on the main checkout. Kepler uses the same folder and does not copy or move your files |
| The workspace's branch | The same branch, in that worktree |
| The workspace's chats | The task's sessions. Open one to continue the chat where it left off |
| The workspace's notes | A note on the task, titled **Notes from Conductor** |
| The workspace's target branch | The worktree's merge target |

A chat continues only if its agent's history is on your Mac and Kepler supports that agent. The workspace list marks a chat that Kepler cannot continue. If a workspace fails to import, the title bar chip counts it, and its card offers **Retry**.

***

## What to do next in Kepler

- **Start new work from your issues.** Connect your tracker and start tasks from the **Todo** view, with the issue attached. See [Start a Coding Agent from a Jira or GitHub Issue and Take It to a Pull Request](/kepler/kepler-start-agent-from-issue-to-pull-request).
- **Run Actions.** Run **Plan**, **Implement**, **Review**, or your own Actions on a task instead of retyping prompts. See [Actions](/kepler/actions).
- **Review each task's changes.** Read the diff in the **Changes** overlay, send comments back to the agent, and commit. See [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes).
- **Set up new worktrees.** Run a setup command each time Kepler creates a worktree with **Run on worktree creation**, and copy git-ignored files such as `.env` with a `.worktreeinclude` file. See [Repository Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories) and [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

***

## Common questions

Short answers about moving from Conductor to Kepler.

### Can I move my Conductor workspaces to Kepler?

On macOS, choose **File → Import from Another App…**, pick **Conductor**, tick the workspaces, and click **Import *N* workspaces**. Each workspace becomes a task in the same folder and on the same branch.

### Do my Conductor chats come with me?

A chat comes with you when its agent history is on your Mac and Kepler supports its agent, such as Claude Code and Codex. Each chat becomes a session on the task, and you continue it where it left off.

### Can I import from Conductor on Windows or Linux?

Kepler imports Conductor workspaces only on a Mac, because Conductor runs only on macOS.

### Does importing change anything in Conductor?

No. Kepler reads Conductor's workspaces and does not change or move your files. Both apps then point at the same folders, branches, and chat history, so continue each chat in 1 app only.

### Which other apps can Kepler import from?

Kepler can also import workspaces from Orca, T3 Code, herdr, and Vibe Kanban, in the same **Import from another app** dialog. See [From another agent app](/kepler/create-task#from-another-agent-app).

***

## Related pages

- [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#from-another-agent-app)
- [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources)
- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions)
- [Actions](/kepler/actions)
- [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes)
- [Getting Started with Kepler](/kepler/kepler-getting-started)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

# Run Multiple Coding Agents in Parallel on Windows with Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-run-coding-agents-in-parallel-on-windows/
product: Kepler
feature: Parallel Agents on Windows
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken installs natively on Windows, so you can run Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents in parallel without a Mac or WSL. Each task gets its own worktree, a private Git working copy, so agents that run at the same time never change each other's files.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Installing Kepler on Windows, installing coding agents there, and running several agents at once
- Prerequisite: Windows 10 and later, on 64-bit or ARM64, and a GitKraken account to sign in to Kepler
- Prerequisite: Your own account for each coding agent you use, such as a Claude or ChatGPT plan
- Limits: Auggie, Pi, and OpenCode need Node.js on Windows. OpenCode installs only through npm on Windows
- Limits: A worktree separates files only. Agents still share ports, databases, and other local services. See [What a worktree does not separate](#what-a-worktree-does-not-separate)

***

## Quick Start

1. Go to [gitkraken.com/kepler/download](https://www.gitkraken.com/kepler/download), download the Windows installer for your computer (64-bit or ARM64), and run it.
2. Launch Kepler and click **Sign in with GitKraken**.
3. In **Choose your coding agents**, switch on Claude Code and Codex. To install an agent you do not have yet, click its tile.
4. In **Bring in your repos**, check the repositories you work in, then click the button that adds them.
5. Click **New task** or press **Ctrl/⌘ + N**, write a prompt, attach a repository with **Add repo or folder**, and click **Start**. Kepler creates a worktree for the task and starts the agent in it.
6. Start a second task the same way, and pick another agent in the **New task** composer. Both agents now work at the same time, each in its own worktree.

***

## How to install Kepler on Windows

Kepler has installers for 2 Windows architectures:

| Installer | For |
|---|---|
| 64-bit | Windows 10 and later on an Intel or AMD processor |
| ARM64 | Windows 10 and later on an ARM processor |

1. Go to [gitkraken.com/kepler/download](https://www.gitkraken.com/kepler/download) and pick the Windows installer for your processor.
2. Run the installer.
3. Launch Kepler and sign in. A guided start then helps you set up agents and repositories.

Kepler runs directly on Windows. You do not need WSL, a virtual machine, or a Mac to use it. See [Getting Started with Kepler](/kepler/kepler-getting-started#install-kepler) for the other platforms.

***

## How to install coding agents on Windows

Kepler supports 9 coding agents on Windows. When an agent is missing, open **Settings → Agents**, click **Install** on its row, and pick an install method. Kepler runs the install command for you and shows its output. After the install, Kepler offers to sign you in to the agent.

| Agent | Install methods on Windows | Note for Windows |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Native installer, winget, npm (global) | Kepler marks npm **Deprecated by Anthropic** |
| **Codex** | Standalone installer, npm (global) | None |
| **GitHub Copilot** | winget, npm (global) | None |
| **Cursor** | Native installer | None |
| **Auggie** | npm (global) | Needs Node.js |
| **OpenCode** | npm (global) | Needs Node.js. npm is the only Windows method |
| **Grok Build** | Native installer | None |
| **Pi** | Native installer, npm (global) | Needs Node.js for both methods. Runs in Terminal only |
| **Antigravity** | Native installer | Google's agent |

Kepler offers a method only when the tool it runs, such as winget or npm, is installed. When an agent needs Node.js and it is missing, Kepler says so and offers **Get Node.js**. Install Node.js, then click **Rescan**.

If you installed an agent yourself and Kepler did not find it, open the agent's **Set up** dialog, enter the program's full path under **Already installed?**, and click **Use this**. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations#install-an-agent).

***

## How to run agents in parallel

In Kepler, the unit of work is a task. Each task holds its own sessions, and each repository you attach to it gets its own worktree. To run several agents at once, start one task per piece of work:

1. Click **New task** or press **Ctrl/⌘ + N**.
2. Write the prompt, and attach the repository with **Add repo or folder**.
3. Under **Agent**, pick the agent for this task, such as Claude Code.
4. Click **Start**.
5. Repeat for the next piece of work, with the same agent or another one, such as Codex.

You can attach the same repository to several tasks. Each task gets its own worktree on its own branch, so 2 agents can change the same repository at the same time.

To follow every agent at once, use the Dashboard. Kepler notifies you when an agent needs you, for example to answer a permission request. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#notifications).

***

## How a worktree per task keeps agents apart

A worktree is a private Git working copy for one task. Agents make their changes there, so nothing they do touches the checkout you work in, and agents in different tasks never change each other's files. This works the same on native Windows as on macOS and Linux.

**Isolated worktree** is the default for new tasks. You can change the default in **Settings → Tasks → Where new tasks make changes**, and change it for each repository in each task. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#worktrees-and-working-in-place).

A new worktree has none of your Git-ignored files, such as `.env` or `node_modules`. To set up each new worktree automatically, see [Set Up Every New Agent Worktree Automatically](/kepler/kepler-set-up-agent-worktrees-automatically).

### What a worktree does not separate

A worktree gives each task its own copy of the files, and nothing else. Agents in different tasks still share:

- **Ports.** Two worktrees that start the same dev server on the same port collide.
- **Databases and other local services.** Agents that point at the same database read and write the same data.
- **Caches and files outside the repository**, such as a global package cache.

To give each worktree its own port or database, use a repository command that runs when Kepler creates the worktree. See [Set Up Every New Agent Worktree Automatically](/kepler/kepler-set-up-agent-worktrees-automatically#how-to-give-each-worktree-its-own-port-or-database).

***

## When to use WSL 2 instead

Run agents natively on Windows when your project builds and runs on Windows. Use a WSL 2 distro when your project needs a Linux toolchain, such as build scripts written for bash.

In Kepler, a WSL 2 distro is a remote environment. Your agents, worktrees, and terminals run inside the distro, while you work from the Kepler window on Windows. It needs no credentials and no extra setup:

1. Open **Settings → Remote environments**.
2. Find your distro under **Found on this machine**, and click **Add**.
3. Connect to it from the environment chip in the title bar.

Kepler lists WSL **version 2** distros only. Install each agent inside the distro, because agents in a remote environment run there. See [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments#wsl-environments).

***

## Common questions

Short answers about running coding agents on Windows with Kepler.

### Does Kepler work on Windows, or is it Mac only?

Kepler works on Windows. It has a native Windows installer for Windows 10 and later, on 64-bit and ARM64. It also runs on macOS and Linux.

### Can I run Claude Code and Codex at the same time on Windows?

Claude Code and Codex can run at the same time on Windows. Start one task for each, and pick Claude Code for one and Codex for the other. Each task gets its own worktree, so the 2 agents never change each other's files.

### Do I need WSL to run coding agents on Windows?

You do not need WSL. All 9 agents that Kepler supports install and run on native Windows. Use WSL 2 only when your project needs a Linux toolchain.

### How do I stop parallel agents from overwriting each other's work?

Leave **Isolated worktree** on, which is the default. Each task then works in its own worktree on its own branch. When the work is done, review and merge each branch on its own. See [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes).

### Why does my second agent's dev server fail to start?

When 2 worktrees start a dev server on the same port, the second server can fail to start. A worktree separates files only. Give each worktree its own port with a repository command. See [Set Up Every New Agent Worktree Automatically](/kepler/kepler-set-up-agent-worktrees-automatically#how-to-give-each-worktree-its-own-port-or-database).

***

## Related pages

- [Getting Started with Kepler](/kepler/kepler-getting-started)
- [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations)
- [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources)
- [Create a task](/kepler/create-task)
- [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments)
- [Set Up Every New Agent Worktree Automatically](/kepler/kepler-set-up-agent-worktrees-automatically)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

# Set Up Every New Agent Worktree Automatically in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-set-up-agent-worktrees-automatically/
product: Kepler
feature: Worktree Setup
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken repeats your worktree setup every time it creates a worktree for an agent. You set it up once per repository: a `.worktreeinclude` file copies Git-ignored files such as `.env` into each new worktree, and repository commands set to **Run on worktree creation** install dependencies in the background, for Claude Code, Codex, or any other agent.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Preparing every new worktree that Kepler creates for a task: ignored files, dependency installs, and per-worktree settings such as a port or a database name
- Prerequisite: The repository is added to Kepler, in **Settings → Repositories**
- Limits: Kepler copies only files that Git ignores in the new worktree, and never overwrites a file that is already there
- Limits: Setup commands run one at a time, in list order. If one fails, Kepler skips the rest. Each command has a 10-minute timeout
- Limits: A worktree separates files only. Ports, databases, and caches stay shared unless your setup gives each worktree its own

***

## Quick Start

1. At the root of your repository, create a file named `.worktreeinclude` and list the Git-ignored files each worktree needs, such as `.env`, in `.gitignore` syntax.
2. In Kepler, open **Settings → Repositories** and open the repository's page.
3. Under **Commands**, click **Add command**. Name it, such as *Install deps*, and enter the install command, such as `pnpm install`.
4. Tick **Run on worktree creation** and click **Add command** to save it.
5. Start a task with Claude Code or Codex. Kepler creates the worktree, copies the files from `.worktreeinclude`, and runs your setup commands in it.

***

## How to copy .env and other ignored files into each worktree

A new worktree is a clean checkout. It has none of the Git-ignored files in your own checkout, such as `.env`, local config files, or certificates.

To copy them into every new worktree:

1. Create a file named `.worktreeinclude` at the root of the repository.
2. List the files and folders to copy, in the same format as `.gitignore`.

For example:

```text
.env
.env.development
config/local.json
certs/
```

When Kepler creates a worktree, it copies the matching files from your checkout into it, before any setup command runs and before the agent receives your prompt.

Kepler copies a file only when Git also ignores it in the new worktree, so an agent cannot commit a copied secret by mistake. Kepler never overwrites a file that is already in the worktree. You can commit `.worktreeinclude`, so teammates who use Kepler get the same list. See [Copy ignored files into new worktrees](/kepler/settings-repositories#copy-ignored-files-into-new-worktrees).

***

## How to install dependencies in each new worktree

A new worktree has no `node_modules`, virtual environment, or build output. Save the setup steps once as repository commands:

1. Open **Settings → Repositories** and open the repository's page.
2. Under **Commands**, click **Add command**.
3. Enter a name, such as *Install deps*, and the command, such as `pnpm install`.
4. Tick **Run on worktree creation**.
5. Click **Add command**, or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Enter**. The command shows a **Runs on creation** chip.

Add one command for each step, and drag the rows into the order they need to run. Each time Kepler creates a worktree for the repository, it runs these commands one at a time, in list order, in the new worktree's folder.

The commands run in the background, so the agent can start while an install is still running. If a command fails, Kepler shows **Worktree setup failed** with the command's name and its error, and skips the commands after it. The worktree stays. To fix it, correct the command, then right-click the worktree in the task's context panel and choose **Run command here**. On Windows, **Run command here** runs the command in a PowerShell terminal, while setup commands run in Command Prompt.

**Which shell runs the commands.** On macOS and Linux, each command runs through your login shell, so tools set up in your shell profile, such as `nvm`, are available. On Windows, each command runs in Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`). Write the command for the shell of the computer, or of the remote environment, where the worktree is created.

**Variables.** A command's **Variables** menu inserts `<WORKTREE_PATH>` (the new worktree's folder), `<REPOSITORY_PATH>` (your main repository folder), `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` and `<SOURCE_PATH>`. Kepler fills them in when the command runs. See [Per-repository commands](/kepler/settings-repositories#per-repository-commands).

***

## How to give each worktree its own port or database

Worktrees separate files, and nothing else. When agents in 2 worktrees start the same dev server on the same port, the second server can fail to start. When they point at the same database, they read and write the same data.

To keep them apart, add a setup command that writes per-worktree settings into a Git-ignored file in the new worktree, such as `.env.local`. Your app then reads its port and database name from that file.

This command works in both shells. It runs Node.js, picks a port between 3000 and 3999, and names the database after the worktree's folder:

```bash
node -e "const p=require('path');require('fs').appendFileSync('.env.local','PORT='+(3000+Math.floor(Math.random()*1000))+'\nDATABASE_NAME=app_'+p.basename(process.cwd())+'\n')"
```

Make sure `.env.local` is in `.gitignore`. Then add a later command that creates the database, using your own tool, such as `pnpm db:create`.

> **Tip:** A random port can still match a port another worktree picked. If your dev server can choose a free port by itself, prefer that.

***

## Example setup to copy

This setup prepares a Node.js repository for parallel agents. Adjust the file names and commands to your project.

`.worktreeinclude` at the repository's root:

```text
.env
config/local.json
```

Commands in **Settings → Repositories**, each with **Run on worktree creation** ticked, in this order:

| Name | Command |
|---|---|
| Install deps | `pnpm install` |
| Worktree settings | `node -e "const p=require('path');require('fs').appendFileSync('.env.local','PORT='+(3000+Math.floor(Math.random()*1000))+'\nDATABASE_NAME=app_'+p.basename(process.cwd())+'\n')"` |
| Create database | `pnpm db:create` |

A command such as `pnpm dev` that you want to run by hand stays unticked. You run it from **Run command here** when you need it.

***

## What a worktree does not separate

A worktree gives each task its own copy of the repository's files. Tasks still share everything outside the worktree's folder:

| Shared | What happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Ports** | Two dev servers on the same port collide | Write a port per worktree in a setup command |
| **Databases and other local services** | Agents read and write the same data | Write a database name per worktree, and create it in a setup command |
| **Caches and files outside the repository** | A global package cache or a file in your home folder is the same for every worktree | Keep per-task files inside the repository, in Git-ignored paths |

See [What a worktree does not separate](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#what-a-worktree-does-not-separate).

***

## Common questions

Short answers about setting up agent worktrees automatically in Kepler.

### How do I copy my .env file into every new worktree?

List `.env` in a `.worktreeinclude` file at the repository's root. Kepler copies it from your checkout into each new worktree before the agent receives your prompt. Kepler copies it only while Git ignores it.

### Can Kepler run npm install or pnpm install when it creates a worktree?

Yes. Add the install as a repository command in **Settings → Repositories**, and tick **Run on worktree creation**.

### Does the agent wait for the install to finish?

No. Setup commands run in the background, and the agent can start before they finish. The files from `.worktreeinclude` are in place before the agent receives your prompt.

### What happens when a setup command fails?

Kepler shows **Worktree setup failed** with the command and its error, and skips the commands after it. The worktree stays. Fix the command, then run it again with **Run command here**. On Windows, that runs it in PowerShell.

### Does this work for Claude Code, Codex, and other agents?

Yes. The setup belongs to the repository, so it runs for every new worktree, whichever agent the task uses.

### Does this work on Windows?

Yes. On Windows, setup commands run in Command Prompt, so write them for `cmd.exe`, or use a command that works in both shells, such as the `node -e` example above.

***

## Related pages

- [Tasks and Resources: Make a new worktree ready to build](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#make-a-new-worktree-ready-to-build)
- [Settings: Per-repository commands](/kepler/settings-repositories#per-repository-commands)
- [Settings: Copy ignored files into new worktrees](/kepler/settings-repositories#copy-ignored-files-into-new-worktrees)
- [Run Multiple Coding Agents in Parallel on Windows](/kepler/kepler-run-coding-agents-in-parallel-on-windows)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

---
# Manage Claude Code and Codex Sessions Across Accounts and SSH Hosts in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-manage-agents-across-accounts-and-ssh-hosts/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Accounts and Remote Environments
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken manages your Claude Code and Codex sessions across several accounts and SSH hosts in 1 app. You add each account once in **Settings → Agents**, pick the account when you start a session, and add each remote server in **Settings → Remote environments**. Sessions on a server run there and keep running when you disconnect.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Several signed-in accounts for 1 agent, choosing the account for each session, moving a conversation to another account, and running agent sessions on SSH hosts.
- Agents with several accounts: Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build.
- Moving a conversation to another account: Claude Code and Codex only, and only between accounts that share history with the CLI.
- SSH hosts: Kepler installs itself on the host over SSH. The agent you want to run must also be installed and signed in on the host.
- Limits: SSH hosts and WSL distros need the Kepler desktop app. Kepler in a browser cannot connect to them.
- Limits: Each Kepler window works on 1 machine at a time. Open 1 window per machine to watch several machines side by side.

***

## Quick Start

1. Open **Settings → Agents** and click the **Claude Code** or **Codex** row.
2. Under **Accounts**, click **Add account**, name the account, and sign in. Repeat for each account.
3. Open **Settings → Remote environments**, click **Add machine**, and follow the steps to add your SSH host.
4. Click **Connect** on the host. In the window connected to the host, install and sign in to Claude Code or Codex in **Settings → Agents**.
5. Start a task. In the **Agent** list, pick the agent and the account in 1 click.
6. To move a running conversation to another account, use **Switch account** on the session's row menu.

***

## How to add several accounts to 1 agent

Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build can each have more than 1 signed-in account, such as a work account and a personal account.

1. Open **Settings → Agents** and click the agent's row.
2. Under **Accounts**, click **Add account**.
3. For Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot, choose how the account handles conversation history:
   - **Share with the CLI**: the account reads the same conversations as the agent's own login. Pick this to move conversations between accounts later.
   - **Keep separate**: the account keeps its own conversations.
4. Sign in.

The first row is the agent's own login. The account badged **Default** is the one new sessions use. Each account keeps its own sign-in and shares your skills, commands, and settings. Give each added account a color to tell sessions apart: the color tints the agent icon on session tabs.

With 2 or more accounts, the list is in priority order. To reorder it, drag a row by its handle, or use **Move to top**, **Move up**, or **Move down** in the row's menu. When you pick no account, a new session starts on the first account from the top with usage left. At a usage limit, Kepler moves to, or suggests, the first account from the top with usage left. To skip an account at a usage limit, clear **Use at a usage limit** in its menu. The row then reads **Skipped at a usage limit**.

See [Several accounts for one agent](/kepler/agent-sessions#several-accounts-for-one-agent) for every account control.

***

## How to choose the account for a session

When an agent has 2 or more accounts, the **Agent** list shows 1 row per account, labeled with the account name. Pick the row in the **New task** window or in a new session tab, and the session runs under that account. On a session that already started, picking another account in its **Agent** list moves the conversation instead. See [How to move a conversation to another account](#how-to-move-a-conversation-to-another-account).

To add an account without leaving the list, click **Add another *agent* account** at the foot of the list, such as **Add another Claude Code account**. It opens that agent's add-account dialog in Settings. The list offers it only for agents that take several accounts.

Each session runs under 1 account. Session tabs name the account, so you can see which account each session uses.

***

## How to move a conversation to another account

Move a Claude Code or Codex conversation to another account when an account reaches its usage limit, or when you started on the wrong account. The conversation stays the same.

1. Open the session's row menu and select **Switch account**.
2. Pick the account. Kepler restarts the agent on that account with the same conversation.

When an account reaches its usage limit, a bar on the session's composer says which limit and when it resets. The bar offers these choices:

- **Continue on** *account* picks up where the conversation stopped.
- A new session on another account reads this conversation first.
- **Wait** continues the conversation when the account resets.

You can also pick the account in the **Agent** list of the session's **Agent settings**, or click the account badge beside the session's plan usage meter.

The move works only between accounts that share history with the CLI. An account that keeps its own history shows as **Separate history** in the list, because it cannot read the conversation. Sessions started outside Kepler cannot move to another account.

See [Moving a session to another account](/kepler/agent-sessions#moving-a-session-to-another-account).

***

## How to add an SSH host

1. Open **Settings → Remote environments** and click **Add machine**. To add a host that is already in your `~/.ssh/config`, click **Add** next to it under **Found on this machine** instead.
2. Enter the **Host**, and optionally the **Name**, **User**, and **Port**.
3. Choose how Kepler signs in: an existing key, your SSH agent, your SSH config, a password, or a key Kepler generates for this host.
4. Check the host's fingerprint and click **Trust and continue**.
5. After Kepler tests the connection, click **Add**, then click **Connect** on the host.

Kepler installs itself on the host over SSH, so you do not need to set up Kepler there first. The agent is different: Claude Code or Codex must be installed on the host. In a window connected to the host, **Settings → Agents** lists the host's agents. If an agent shows **Not installed**, click **Install** to install it on the host, then sign in. The sign-in page opens in the browser on your own computer, and Kepler saves the sign-in on the host.

See [Add an SSH host](/kepler/remote-environments#add-an-ssh-host) for every step and sign-in option.

***

## Where your sessions run

In a window connected to an SSH host, the agent sessions, terminals, worktrees, and Git operations all run on the host. Your own computer runs only the Kepler window.

Sessions belong to the host, not to the window. If you close the window, lose the network, or put your laptop to sleep, the sessions keep running on the host. When you connect again, Kepler lists them, and you pick up where you left off.

See [What runs where](/kepler/remote-environments#what-runs-where).

***

## How to see all of it in one place

Each Kepler window shows 1 machine's tasks and sessions on its Dashboard, including which sessions need you. Use these to cover your computer and every server:

- **Switch machines from the title bar.** The chip after **New task**, at the left of the title bar, shows which machine the window works on: a computer icon for this computer, or a host name. Click it and pick a machine under **Switch to**.
- **Open a window per machine.** In the chip's menu, click the window icon next to a host to open it in a new window. Keep 1 window on your computer and 1 on each server.
- **Manage every machine in Settings.** **Settings → Remote environments** lists **Your machines**, whether each one is connected, and how many windows use it.

To keep track of which session needs you on each machine, see [Keep Track of Several Claude Code and Codex Sessions](/kepler/kepler-track-multiple-agent-sessions).

***

## Common questions

Short answers about agent accounts and SSH hosts in Kepler.

### Can I use 2 Claude Code accounts at the same time?

Sessions on different accounts run side by side. Add both accounts in **Settings → Agents**, then pick a different account for each session.

### Can I run Claude Code on 1 account and Codex on another at the same time?

Each agent has its own accounts, and each session picks its own agent and account.

### Can I switch accounts when I hit a usage limit?

When an account reaches its limit, the bar on the session's composer offers **Continue on** another account. You can also use **Switch account** on the session's row menu. For Claude Code and Codex, the conversation moves to the other account when both accounts share history with the CLI. Otherwise, the bar offers a new session on another account that reads this conversation first.

### Do I need to install anything on the SSH server?

Not for Kepler: it installs itself over SSH. The agent you want to run, such as Claude Code or Codex, must be installed on the server. Install it from **Settings → Agents** in a window connected to the server.

### Do my sessions stop when I disconnect from the server?

No. Sessions run on the server and keep running after you close the window or lose the connection. Connect again to pick them up.

### Does this work with WSL too?

On Windows, a WSL 2 distribution is a remote environment like an SSH host. See [WSL environments](/kepler/remote-environments#wsl-environments).

***

## Related pages

- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions)
- [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations)
- [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments)
- [Settings](/kepler/settings-environment)
- [Keep Track of Several Claude Code and Codex Sessions](/kepler/kepler-track-multiple-agent-sessions)
- [Quick Answers](/kepler/quick-answers)

---
# Keep Track of Several Claude Code and Codex Sessions in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-track-multiple-agent-sessions/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Sessions
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken keeps track of several Claude Code and Codex sessions in 1 Dashboard, including sessions you start in your own terminal. Give each piece of work its own task, so each one gets its own worktree and branch. The Dashboard then shows which session needs you, and each task's **Changes** group shows what its agent changed.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Following several agent sessions at once, seeing which one needs you, and seeing which one changed what.
- Sessions you start in your own terminal: Kepler lists them while **Show them in Kepler** under **Sessions outside Kepler** is on, which it is by default.
- Limits: Kepler follows a session running in your terminal but does not control it. To answer a question it asks, answer in your terminal, or move the session into Kepler.
- Limits: Sessions that share a worktree also share its changes. To tell their changes apart, give each session its own task.

***

## Quick Start

1. Check that **Show them in Kepler** is on in **Settings → General → Sessions outside Kepler**. It is on by default.
2. Click **New task**, select **Continue a session started outside Kepler**, and pick a Claude Code or Codex session you already started. Kepler puts it in a task.
3. For new work, click **New task**, write the prompt, and pick **Claude Code** or **Codex**. Each new task gets its own worktree.
4. Open the Dashboard's **Tasks** view. Tasks that need you are listed first, under **Needs attention**.
5. To see what a session changed, open its task and click the worktree under **Changes**.

***

## How to follow sessions started in your terminal

Kepler can list the Claude Code and Codex sessions you run in your own terminal, so you can follow them next to the sessions Kepler starts.

1. Open **Settings → General → Sessions outside Kepler**.
2. Check that **Show them in Kepler** is on. It is on by default. Turn it off to stop listing them.

The setting covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Auggie, Grok Build, Pi, and Google Antigravity.

To put a terminal session in a task:

1. Click **New task**, then select **Continue a session started outside Kepler**.
2. Pick the session under **Live now**, or a past one under **Past sessions**. Kepler opens it in a new task.

A session still running in your terminal opens read-only. The bar under its transcript says what it is doing, such as **Running outside Kepler** or **Waiting on you**. When it waits on you, answer in your terminal.

### Take a session over

To carry the session on in Kepler, use the bar under its transcript. You can first pick the account, the mode, and the agent settings there:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Fork** | Copies the conversation into a new Kepler session. Your terminal keeps the original |
| **Continue here** | Carries on the same conversation in Kepler. Close it in your terminal first |

See [Sessions started outside Kepler](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

***

## How to give each task its own worktree

Give each piece of work its own task. By default, each new task makes its changes in its own worktree: a separate copy of the repository on its own branch. Sessions in different tasks do not edit the same files, so you always know which session changed what.

- **Name tasks by the work.** A task's name is what you see on the Dashboard. To rename one, use **Rename task** on its menu.
- **Name sessions by their job.** When a task holds more than 1 session, use **Rename session** on the session's menu, for example "tests" or "review".
- **Start related work as a new task**, not as a second session in the same worktree, when you want to review it separately.

To change where new tasks make their changes, open **Settings → Tasks** and find **Where new tasks make changes**. **Isolated worktree** is the default. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

***

## How to see which session needs you

Kepler shows what needs you on the Dashboard, in the top bar, on each session, in notifications, in the Agent Graph, and through Ask Kepler.

### The Dashboard and its Inbox

The Dashboard's **Tasks** view groups tasks by what each one needs from you. This grouping, **Inbox**, is the default. The first 3 sections are:

| Section | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Needs attention** | A session waits on you, such as a question or a permission request. A failed turn stays here until you open the task |
| **Unread** | A session finished a turn you have not looked at |
| **Running** | An agent is working on it |

Each task row adds a line that says what its session needs, such as **Approval needed for** *tool*, **Asking:** *question*, or **New reply**. See [Inbox](/kepler/arranging-your-work#inbox).

### Tasks that need you, in the top bar

The **Search Kepler** field in the top bar shows how many tasks need you and how many have unread replies. Click it, or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + P**, to open the palette with those tasks first, under **Needs you** and **Unread**, each with what it needs. Click a task to open it at that session, or answer a waiting request from its row. Work waiting on your other machines is listed under **Other machines**. See [Go to a task or file](/kepler/kepler-interface#go-to-a-task-or-file).

To go straight to the next thing, press **F8** (**Go to what needs you next**). Each press opens the next session across your tasks: sessions waiting on you first, then unread replies.

### Session status

Every session shows a colored status on its tab and rows. **Waiting** means it is blocked on you, and says on what, such as **Permission**, **Question**, or **Plan review**. See [Session status](/kepler/agent-sessions#session-status).

### Notifications

Kepler notifies you when a session needs you, replies, or fails. Choose which events notify you in **Settings → Notifications**. See [Notifications](/kepler/agent-sessions#notifications).

### The Agent Graph

The Dashboard's **Agent Graph** view shows every task, session, turn, tool call, and file as a live graph. Its **Needs attention** list names everything waiting on you, most urgent first. See [The Agent Graph](/kepler/agent-graph).

### Ask Kepler

Open **Ask Kepler** and ask **What needs me right now?** Kepler lists what is waiting on you. See [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler).

***

## How to see which session changed what

Each task lists its worktrees under **Changes** in the context panel, on the left of the task page. Click a worktree to open its changes: the files and lines that branch changed. Because each task has its own worktree, the changes you see belong to that task's sessions.

On the Dashboard, a task's preview shows each worktree with chips for its uncommitted files and commits. Click a chip to open that worktree's changes without leaving the Dashboard.

See [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes) to read the diff, comment on it, and commit.

***

## Common questions

The Dashboard follows every task in one place and lists the tasks that wait on you first.

### How do people manage 5 or more Claude Code and Codex sessions at once?

Give each piece of work its own task and worktree, name each task by its work, and check the Dashboard's **Needs attention** section instead of each terminal. Kepler lists the sessions that wait on you first.

### Can Kepler see the Claude Code session I started in my terminal?

Kepler sees it while **Settings → General → Sessions outside Kepler → Show them in Kepler** is on, which it is by default.

### Can I answer a terminal session's question from Kepler?

Kepler follows a session that runs in your terminal but does not control it. Answer in your terminal, or close the session there and click **Continue here** to carry the conversation on in Kepler.

### How do I know which session changed a file?

Open the task and click its worktree under **Changes**. Each task has its own worktree, so the changes there belong to that task's sessions.

### Can 2 agents work in the same repository at once?

Each task gets its own worktree, so Claude Code and Codex can work in the same repository at once, each in its own copy, without editing each other's files.

***

## Related pages

- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions)
- [Create a task](/kepler/create-task)
- [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources)
- [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work)
- [The Agent Graph](/kepler/agent-graph)
- [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler)
- [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes)
