# Approve Coding Agent Requests from Your Phone with Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-approve-agent-requests-from-your-phone/
product: Kepler
feature: Remote Access
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken lets you see what your coding agents are doing and approve their requests from your phone. Turn on Remote Access in Kepler on your computer, scan its QR code with your phone, and answer each permission request from Claude Code, Codex, or any other agent in your phone's browser, with the same choices as on your desktop. Your phone can also notify you when an agent needs you.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Watching agent sessions and answering permission requests, questions, plan reviews, and approval requests from a phone
- Prerequisite: Kepler running on your computer, signed in to your GitKraken account. Your agents keep running on the computer, and the phone shows its interface
- Prerequisite: A phone browser signed in to the same GitKraken account
- Limits: The phone gets notifications only after you turn on **Notify this phone** in Kepler on the phone. On an iPhone, add Kepler to your home screen first

***

## Quick Start

1. In Kepler on your computer, open **Settings → Remote Access** and click **Turn on Remote Access**.
2. In **Name this machine**, keep the name or enter your own, then click **Turn on Remote Access** in the dialog.
3. Scan the QR code with your phone's camera, and sign in with your GitKraken account.
4. In your phone's browser menu, choose the option that adds the page to your home screen, such as Add to Home Screen, to open Kepler like an app.
5. In Kepler on your phone, open **Settings → Notifications** and turn on **Notify this phone**.
6. When an agent stops to ask, answer from the notification, or tap the notification to open the request in Kepler and choose **Approve** or **Deny**.

***

## How to turn on Remote Access

Remote Access opens this Kepler from another device, such as your phone, through your GitKraken account. Your agents, worktrees, and terminals stay on your computer.

1. On your computer, open **Settings → Remote Access**, or hover over the **Remote Access** button in the title bar.
2. Click **Turn on Remote Access**.
3. In **Name this machine**, keep the name Kepler fills in, or enter a name you recognize, then click **Turn on Remote Access** in the dialog.

Remote Access stays on until you turn it off, including after Kepler restarts. By default, Kepler keeps your computer awake while Remote Access is on, so your agents keep working while you are away. To change this, use **Keep this machine awake while agents work** in **Settings → Agents → Keep agents running**. See [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments#turning-on-remote-access).

***

## How to pair your phone

When Remote Access is active, Kepler shows a QR code and a link in **Settings → Remote Access** and in the **Remote Access** popover.

1. Scan the QR code with your phone's camera. To pair another browser instead, click **Copy link** and open the link there.
2. The link opens gitkraken.dev. Sign in with the GitKraken account you use in Kepler.
3. Kepler opens in your phone's browser, in a layout made for phones.

Only your GitKraken account can connect. To disconnect one device, use **Connected devices** in **Settings → Remote Access**. To disconnect every device, click **Turn off Remote Access**.

***

## How to add Kepler to your home screen

To open Kepler like an app, add it to your phone's home screen from the browser's menu, such as Add to Home Screen. Where the browser can install web apps, the Dashboard also offers to install Kepler, and the phone menu has **Install app**. The Kepler icon then opens Kepler full screen, without the browser's address bar and toolbars.

***

## How to get notifications on your phone

Your phone can notify you when a session needs you and you are away from your computer, even while Kepler is closed on the phone. The Dashboard on your phone offers to turn them on: tap **Turn on**. To turn them on from Settings instead:

1. On an iPhone, add Kepler to your home screen first, then open Kepler from its home screen icon.
2. In Kepler on your phone, tap **Menu**, then **Settings**, and open **Notifications**.
3. Under **Notifications on this phone**, turn on **Notify this phone**, and allow notifications when the browser asks.
4. To check that they arrive, tap **Send a test**.

To choose which events reach the phone, use the **Phone** column in **What to notify you about**, in **Settings → Notifications** on your computer. The column appears once a phone gets notifications. When you answer a request on another device, its notification leaves the phone. Turning off Remote Access, or removing the phone from it, stops its notifications.

***

## How to find what waits on you

Kepler marks every task and session that waits on you, so you can find a request as soon as you open Kepler on your phone:

- **A notification.** With **Notify this phone** on, the phone shows a notification when a session needs you. Tap it to open the request. See [How to get notifications on your phone](#how-to-get-notifications-on-your-phone).
- **An alert.** While Kepler is open on the phone, a new permission request, question, plan review, or approval request shows as an alert. A permission alert has **Allow** and **Deny** for a one-time answer, and **View**, which opens the request in its session.
- **The menu.** Tap **Menu**. Under **Recent tasks**, a dot marks each task that waits on you.
- **The task list.** On the Dashboard, a Tasks view grouped by **Inbox** lists the tasks that wait on you under **Needs attention**.
- **The Search Kepler chip.** On the Dashboard's bar and a task's bar, the **Search Kepler** chip shows a count while something waits on you. Tap it to see what needs you first, under **Needs you**. Tap a request there to answer it with **Allow** or **Deny**, or tap **Open session** to open it in an answer sheet.
- **Inside a task.** Tap **Sessions** to go to the session that waits on you.

> **Note:** While **Notify this phone** is off, nothing tells you that an agent is waiting when Kepler is closed on the phone. On your computer, Kepler's desktop notifications still work as usual.

***

## How to answer a permission request

A permission request pins to the top of its session. It names the tool the agent wants to use and shows the call, such as the shell command. Tap one of the buttons:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Allow** | Approves this one call |
| **Allow for this session** | Approves this call and matching calls for the rest of the session |
| **Allow always** | Gives the agent a permanent approval, stored in the agent's own settings |
| **Reject** | Refuses this call |
| **Reject always** | Refuses it permanently |

You see only the choices the agent offers. A session in Terminal mode shows the same card, with **Reject**, **Allow**, and an **Allow always** button for each scope. The agent continues as soon as you answer. If you already answered on another device, Kepler says **Already answered**. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#permission-requests).

A request you open from a notification, or with **Open session** under the **Search Kepler** chip, opens in an answer sheet over its task. The sheet shows the full command or the changes, with **Approve** and **Deny**, and the agent's other choices under **Other ways to answer**. Inside the sheet, **Open session** takes you to the session itself, at the request. When more than one request waits on you, **Previous request** and **Next request** step through them, and the sheet moves to the next one after each answer.

### Answer from the notification

You can answer some requests from the phone's notification, even on the lock screen, without opening Kepler. A short shell command has **Allow** and **Deny**, and an approval request that is not destructive has **Approve** and **Deny**. For anything else, such as a file edit, a long command, or a destructive approval request, tap the notification to answer it in Kepler.

***

## How to answer plans, questions, and approval requests

Other requests wait in the session the same way, and you answer them on the phone as you do on your computer:

- **A plan review.** Read the agent's plan, then **Approve** it or comment and tap **Request changes (*n*)**. See [Reviewing a plan](/kepler/agent-sessions#reviewing-a-plan).
- **A question.** Pick an option, or type your own answer, and submit. See [Multiple-choice and multi-select questions](/kepler/agent-sessions#multiple-choice-and-multi-select-questions).
- **An approval request**, when an agent asks Kepler itself to do something, such as delete a worktree. Tap **Approve** or **Deny**. See [Approval requests](/kepler/agent-sessions#approval-requests).

Questions, approval requests, and plan reviews also open in the answer sheet. For a plan review, the sheet shows the plan with **Approve & implement**. To request changes, open the session. To answer from the notification instead, see [Answer from the notification](#answer-from-the-notification).

To see what an agent did while you were away, open its session and read the conversation, or tap **Changes** to read the changed files.

***

## Common questions

Your agents keep running on your computer while you answer them from your phone.

### Will my phone notify me when an agent needs permission?

Yes, once you turn on **Notify this phone** in **Settings → Notifications** in Kepler on the phone. The phone then notifies you when a session needs you and you are away from your computer, and you can answer some requests from the notification. On an iPhone, add Kepler to your home screen first. See [How to get notifications on your phone](#how-to-get-notifications-on-your-phone).

### Do I need to install an app on my phone?

No. Kepler opens in your phone's browser. To open it like an app, add it to your home screen from the browser's menu.

### Does my computer need to stay on?

Your computer needs to stay on. Your agents run on it, and the phone shows that computer's Kepler. By default, Kepler keeps the computer awake while Remote Access is on, with the setting **Keep this machine awake while agents work** in **Settings → Agents → Keep agents running**.

### Does this work with Claude Code and Codex?

In a Chat session, a permission request shows the same buttons whichever agent raised it, including Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot. A session in Terminal mode shows the same card, with **Reject**, **Allow**, and **Allow always**, and you answer those from the phone too.

### Can someone else open my Kepler from their phone?

No. Only your GitKraken account can connect. You can disconnect any single device in **Connected devices**, or every device with **Turn off Remote Access**.

***

## Related pages

- [Remote Environments: Remote access](/kepler/remote-environments#remote-access-reach-kepler-from-another-device)
- [Remote Environments: Using Kepler on a phone](/kepler/remote-environments#using-kepler-on-a-phone)
- [Agent Sessions: When the agent asks you something](/kepler/agent-sessions#when-the-agent-asks-you-something)
- [Agent Sessions: Notifications](/kepler/agent-sessions#notifications)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

---
# Start a Coding Agent from a Jira or GitHub Issue and Take It to a Pull Request in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-start-agent-from-issue-to-pull-request/
product: Kepler
feature: Tasks
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken starts a coding agent from a GitHub or GitLab issue in 1 click, or from a Jira issue once you add its repository, with the ticket already attached, and takes the work to a pull request. You connect your tracker once, then click the **Action** button on the issue's row in **Todo**. Kepler creates a task, sets up a worktree by default, and starts Claude Code, Codex, or your default agent with the issue's details in place, so you never paste the ticket into a chat.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Going from an issue in a connected tracker to an agent's pull request, inside 1 Kepler task
- Prerequisite: A GitKraken account signed in to Kepler, and a connected issue tracker. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).
- Supported trackers: Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, Trello, Asana, GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab Self-Hosted, Azure DevOps, and Azure DevOps Server.
- Limits: Kepler's **Create pull request** button works for GitHub.com repositories only. On other hosts, the agent opens the pull request, or you open it yourself. Kepler then attaches it to the task.

***

## Quick Start

1. Go to **Settings → Integrations**, find your tracker, such as **Jira** or **GitHub**, under **Issues and pull requests**, and click **Connect**.
2. Open **Todo** and find the issue.
3. Click the issue's **Action** button. The default for an issue is **Plan**. To start coding straight away, pick **Implement** from the chevron.
4. For a GitHub or GitLab issue, Kepler creates the task, attaches the repository and the issue, sets up a worktree by default, and starts the agent. For a Jira, Trello, Asana, or Azure DevOps issue, the issue's panel opens: add the repository, then send.
5. Review the agent's changes and commit them.
6. Have the agent open the pull request with an Action you create from the **Open a pull request** example, or open it yourself. Kepler attaches the pull request to the task.

***

## How to connect your issue tracker

You connect a tracker once, and its issues appear in **Todo** from then on.

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Under **Issues and pull requests**, find the provider and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler on GitKraken's website, which opens in your browser.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge.

For a self-hosted tracker, such as Jira Server / Data Center or GitHub Enterprise, you connect with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted tracker](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#connect-a-self-hosted-tracker).

***

## How to start the agent from the issue

1. Open **Todo**. It lists your issues from every connected tracker.
2. Find the issue's row, and click its **Action** button.

The left half of the button runs the issue's suggested Action. For an issue, that is **Plan**, which has the agent research the code and propose an approach, then wait for your confirmation before it changes anything. The chevron lists the Actions available on issues, such as **Plan** and **Implement**, which has the agent make the changes directly.

For a GitHub or GitLab issue, Kepler uses your local copy of the repository, or clones it, and then does the following:

1. Creates the task.
2. Attaches the repository and the issue.
3. Sets up a worktree by default, so the agent works on its own branch.
4. Starts an agent with the issue's description attached as context.

A Jira issue names no repository, so Kepler cannot pick the code to work on. The same applies to Trello, Asana, and Azure DevOps issues. When you click **Action**, the issue's panel opens, ready to start a new task, and Kepler shows **Add a repository to start**. Add the repository in the panel, then send. If you started work from the same tracker project before, the panel can fill in that repository for you. A Linear issue gets its repository from the GitHub issue it is synced with.

Kepler also saves the issue's description as a note on the task, titled with the issue's key and title. Long descriptions are shortened, with a link to the issue.

From the issue's row, the agent is your default agent, or the agent the Action names. To use another agent, choose the Action in the **New task** window and change the agent before you send. See [Setting an Action's agent](/kepler/actions#setting-an-actions-agent).

***

## How to take the work to a pull request

When the agent finishes, you review and commit its work, open the pull request, and Kepler attaches the pull request to the task.

### Review and commit

When the agent finishes, open the task's worktree and read its changes in the **Changes** overlay. Send fixes back as review comments, then click **Commit…** to stage and commit. See [Review an AI-Written Pull Request Before Your Teammates Do](/kepler/kepler-review-ai-pull-request-before-sharing) and [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes).

### Open the pull request

None of Kepler's built-in Actions opens a pull request. To have the agent open the pull request, create an Action once from the example on the Actions page:

1. Go to **Settings → Actions** and click **New Action**.
2. For **Title**, type `Open a pull request`.
3. For **Prompt**, paste the prompt from [Example: Open a pull request](/kepler/actions#example-open-a-pull-request). It tells the agent to push the branch, open a pull request against its base branch, write the title and description, and stop if the worktree has uncommitted changes.
4. Under **Available on**, tick **Tasks**.
5. Click **Save**.

Then open the task and pick **Open a pull request** from the chevron on the composer's send button. The agent opens the pull request with the tools it has, such as your Git host's command-line tool.

You can also push the branch and open the pull request yourself. For a GitHub.com repository, click **Create pull request** above the **Todo** list and name the two branches. See [Create and manage GitHub pull requests](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#create-and-manage-github-pull-requests). On other hosts, use the host's website or the worktree's terminal.

### Kepler attaches the pull request

When the agent publishes the pull request on one of the worktree's remotes, Kepler attaches it to the task. The task then holds the issue and its pull request together. A pull request you opened yourself can be attached from **Manage resources** at the bottom of the task's context panel. See [Opening a pull request](/kepler/review-changes#opening-a-pull-request).

With the pull request attached, the **Address Feedback** Action is available on the task. When your teammates leave review comments, run it to have the agent work through each one.

***

## How to start agents on new issues automatically

To have Kepler start the agent for you, set up an [automation](/kepler/kepler-automations). An automation runs an Action on a schedule, or when new GitHub or Jira activity matches its query.

***

## Common questions

Short answers about starting a coding agent from an issue in Kepler.

### Can I start a coding agent straight from a Jira issue?

Yes. Connect Jira in **Settings → Integrations**, then click **Action** on the issue's row in **Todo**, add the repository in the issue's panel, then send. Kepler starts the agent with the issue's description attached as context.

### Which issue trackers does Kepler support?

Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, Trello, Asana, GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab Self-Hosted, Azure DevOps, and Azure DevOps Server. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

### Do I have to copy the ticket into the chat?

No. Starting from the issue's row in **Todo** attaches the issue's description as context, and Kepler saves it as a note on the task.

### Can the agent open the pull request by itself?

Yes. Create an Action from the **Open a pull request** example on the [Actions](/kepler/actions#example-open-a-pull-request) page and run it on the task. Kepler attaches the pull request when the agent publishes it.

### Which agent does the work?

Your default agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, unless the Action names another agent. To use another agent, choose the Action in the **New task** window and change the agent before you send.

***

## Related pages

- [Create a task](/kepler/create-task)
- [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations)
- [Actions](/kepler/actions)
- [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes)
- [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations)
- [Automations](/kepler/kepler-automations)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

# Review an AI-Written Pull Request Before Your Teammates Do, in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-review-ai-pull-request-before-sharing/
product: Kepler
feature: Review Changes
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Kepler by GitKraken gives you a review step between an agent's work and your teammates. You read every changed line in the Changes overlay, send review comments back to the agent, have a second agent review the work, and only then open the pull request. The work stays in the task's worktree while you review it, whether Claude Code, Codex, or another agent wrote it.

## Requirements and limits

- Scope: Reviewing an agent's uncommitted or committed work in a Kepler task before you open a pull request
- Prerequisite: A task whose agent has made changes in its worktree. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).
- Opening the pull request: the agent opens it, or you do. For a GitHub.com repository, you can also click **Create pull request** on the **Todo** list. See [Create and manage GitHub pull requests](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#create-and-manage-github-pull-requests).
- Limits: Review comments you write in Kepler go to the agent. Kepler does not post them to your Git host.
- Second agent's review: a report, not an approval. You still decide what to change.

***

## Quick Start

1. **Restate the problem.** Ask the agent for a summary of what it changed and what it did not test, with an Action you create from the **Prepare for review** example.
2. **Read every changed line.** Open the task's worktree and read the diff in the **Changes** overlay.
3. **Send fixes back.** Comment on the lines that need work, then click **Send comments (*n*)**.
4. **Prove it works.** Ask the agent to run the tests in the session, and read the commands and results it reports.
5. **Get a second opinion.** Run the built-in **Review** Action with a different agent, such as Codex for work Claude Code wrote.
6. **Open the pull request.** Commit, then open the pull request yourself or with an Action you create from the **Open a pull request** example.

***

## How to restate what the change does

Start from what the change is supposed to do, so you can judge the diff against it. Kepler does not ship an Action for this. The [Actions](/kepler/actions#example-prepare-for-review) page has an example, **Prepare for review**, that you create once and then run on any task.

To create it:

1. Go to **Settings → Actions** and click **New Action**.
2. For **Title**, type `Prepare for review`.
3. For **Prompt**, paste the example prompt from [Example: Prepare for review](/kepler/actions#example-prepare-for-review). It asks the agent what the change does, which files it changed and why, which tests it ran, and what it did not test, and tells it to change no files.
4. Under **Available on**, tick **Tasks**.
5. Click **Save**.

To run it, open the task and pick **Prepare for review** from the chevron on the composer's send button. The summary is the agent's own account. Check each point against the diff before you trust it.

***

## How to read every changed line

The agent makes its changes in the task's worktree. To read them:

1. Open the task, and open the worktree from the **Changes** group in the context panel.
2. Click a file, or choose **Open changes** from the worktree's menu, to open the **Changes** overlay.
3. Read each file's diff. The file tree beside it lists every file the agent touched.

See [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes#the-changes-overlay) for the overlay's views, layouts, and keyboard controls.

***

## How to send fixes back to the agent

When a line needs work, comment on it instead of fixing it yourself or retyping the location in the chat.

1. In the **Changes** overlay, hover over a line and click the **+** beside its line number. To comment on a range, **Shift**-click the last line.
2. Type your note.
3. Click **Add comment** to queue it, or **Send now** to send it to the agent at once.
4. When you finish the file, click **Send comments (*n*)** in the overlay's header to send every queued comment.

Each comment reaches the agent with its file, lines, the code, and your note. The agent can reply to each comment, and you resolve the comment when it is handled. See [Review comments](/kepler/review-changes#review-comments).

***

## How to prove the change works

A diff that reads well can still fail. Ask the agent in the task's session to run the tests and tell you the commands and the results. If you created **Prepare for review**, its summary already lists the commands the agent ran and what it did not test. Ask for tests for anything on the "not tested" list before you move on.

***

## How to get a second agent's review

An agent that did not write the code is less likely to repeat the author's mistakes. Kepler ships a built-in **Review** Action. It reviews the uncommitted work in the worktree, or the attached pull request if there is one.

By default **Review** runs on your default agent. To have a different agent review, set its agent once:

1. Go to **Settings → Actions**, and click **Review** under **All Actions**.
2. In the **Agent** field, pick a preset for a different agent from the one that writes your code, or choose **Custom agent settings** and pick that agent.
3. Click **Save**.

Then open the task and pick **Review** from the chevron on the composer's send button. To use a different reviewer only once, pick the agent when you run **Review**. See [Review with a different agent](/kepler/actions#review-with-a-different-agent).

The review is a report. Read it in the session, and send the agent that wrote the code the changes you agree with.

***

## How to open the pull request

When you are satisfied, commit the work. In the **Changes** overlay, click **Commit…** on the **Working changes** row to stage and commit it. See [Staging and committing](/kepler/review-changes#staging-and-committing).

Then open the pull request in one of these ways:

- **Write it yourself.** Push the branch and open the pull request on your Git host's website, or with a command in the worktree's terminal. Writing the description yourself is the last check that you understand the change.
- **Use Create pull request.** For a GitHub.com repository, push the branch, then click **Create pull request** on the **Todo** list. See [Create and manage GitHub pull requests](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#create-and-manage-github-pull-requests).
- **Have the agent open it.** Kepler does not ship an Action for this. Create one from the [Open a pull request](/kepler/actions#example-open-a-pull-request) example in **Settings → Actions**, then run it on the task. The example tells the agent to stop if the worktree has uncommitted changes, and to end the description with a line that says an AI coding agent helped write the change and a person reviewed it.

When the agent publishes the pull request, Kepler attaches it to the task. A pull request you open yourself can be attached from **Manage resources**. See [Opening a pull request](/kepler/review-changes#opening-a-pull-request).

***

## Common questions

Short answers about reviewing an AI-written pull request in Kepler.

### How do I review an AI-written PR myself before I send it to a teammate?

In Kepler, read every changed line in the task's **Changes** overlay, send review comments back to the agent, ask it to run the tests, and run the built-in **Review** Action with a second agent. Open the pull request only after that.

### Can a different AI agent review the code that Claude Code wrote?

Set the **Agent** field of the built-in **Review** Action to Codex or another agent in **Settings → Actions**, or pick the agent when you run **Review**.

### Does Kepler post my review comments to GitHub?

No. Review comments in Kepler go to the agent in the task's session. Your teammates see only the pull request you open.

### Is there a "Prepare for review" or "Open a pull request" button in Kepler?

No. Both are examples on the [Actions](/kepler/actions) page. You create each one once as your own Action in **Settings → Actions**, and then it appears in the list of Actions on every task. For a GitHub.com repository, you can also open the pull request yourself with **Create pull request** on the **Todo** list.

### Can I mark the pull request as AI-assisted?

Write a note in the description yourself, or use an Action created from the **Open a pull request** example, which ends the description with a line that says an AI coding agent helped write the change and a person reviewed it.

***

## Related pages

- [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes)
- [Actions](/kepler/actions)
- [Create a task](/kepler/create-task)
- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions)
- [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations)
- [The Task View](/kepler/task-view)
- [Kepler Quick Answers: Running Coding Agents](/kepler/quick-answers)

# Agent Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/agent-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Settings → Agents** to install the coding agents you already use, sign in to them, and choose how they run in Kepler. You sign in with your own agent account, and Kepler adds no markup on the agents you bring.

Kepler supports 9 agents. You can also add any other agent that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), or whose command-line interface you want to run inside a task.

***

## Supported agents

Each agent has a row under **Settings → Agents → Your agents**. Click a row to open the agent's own page:

| Agent | Name in Settings | How Kepler runs it | Run modes | Multiple accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Claude Code | Your installed `claude` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **Codex** | Codex | Your installed `codex` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **GitHub Copilot** | GitHub Copilot | Your installed `copilot` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **OpenCode** | OpenCode | Your installed `opencode` CLI, v2 | Chat or Terminal | No |
| **Pi** | Pi | Your installed `pi` CLI, in its own terminal interface | Terminal only | No |
| **Auggie** | Auggie | Your installed `auggie` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **Google Antigravity** | Antigravity | Your installed `agy` CLI | Chat or Terminal | No |
| **Cursor** | Cursor | Your installed `cursor-agent` CLI | Chat or Terminal | No |
| **Grok Build** | Grok Build | Your installed `grok` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |

**Auggie** is Augment's coding agent. Like Claude Code and Codex, it reports plan usage back to Kepler, but only as a credit balance rather than usage windows. Google Antigravity reports a percentage used for each limit on the selected model. Those limits include its 5-hour and weekly windows. To learn about the plan usage meter, see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#usage-indicators).

Kepler asks each agent's provider for plan usage, through the agent's own sign-in. If an account row on the agent's page shows **Turn on usage checks**, click it to turn these checks back on.

**Grok Build** is xAI's coding agent. It signs in through your browser, or you can supply an xAI API key.

**Google Antigravity runs the `agy` CLI in both modes.** Chat needs Antigravity CLI 1.5.0 or newer. With an older CLI, Kepler asks you to update it in **Settings → Agents**.

**Pi is terminal-only.** Kepler runs Pi's own interface in a terminal inside the task. Kepler does not check Pi's sign-in. Pi uses its own sign-in (`/login`, or the provider API-key environment variables it reads directly).

With Pi 1.x, a session gets the task's context and Kepler's workspace tools, and your own Pi configuration stays as it was. With other Pi versions, Kepler pastes the task's context into the session instead. A Pi session resumes where it left off.

**OpenCode needs version 2.** Kepler does not start a session on an OpenCode 1 binary. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes in OpenCode 2.

**Auggie 1.2.1 and the older 0.36 and 0.37 builds both run in Kepler.** A conversation continues only on the Auggie generation that started it. To continue a conversation from 0.36 or 0.37, which Kepler marks **Auggie legacy**, select an Auggie 0.37.0 program under **Which Auggie Kepler runs** on Auggie's page.

**Kepler's tools in Terminal mode.** If a **Terminal** session shows **No Kepler tools** on its status bar, choose **Continue in Chat** from the session menu to give the agent Kepler's workspace tools. These agents get them in Terminal mode too, without any change to your own config:

- Claude Code
- Pi
- OpenCode 2.1.1 or newer
- Google Antigravity 1.5.3 or newer

**Waking an idle Terminal session.** When a new report reaches an idle Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, or Auggie session in Terminal mode, Kepler wakes it to read the report. Kepler does not wake a session whose status bar shows **No Kepler tools**. To wake a session, Kepler can type a one-line note into the agent's input, but only when the input is empty. To turn this off, clear **Wake idle terminal agents to read new reports** in **Settings → Agents → Idle agents**.

**Folder trust.** In a repository, worktree, or folder you marked **Trusted** in Kepler, these sessions skip the CLI's own trust question:

- In Terminal mode: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, Pi, and Google Antigravity
- In Chat: Claude Code and Grok Build

A worktree also inherits the trust you already gave its repository. See [Trust a repository](/kepler/settings-repositories#trust-a-repository).

To choose between **Chat** and **Terminal** for an agent, see [Run modes](#run-modes).

These 2 agents need a recent build to run in **Chat**:

| Agent | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **GitHub Copilot** | CLI v1.0 or newer |
| **Cursor CLI** | A build from early 2026 or newer |

Kepler checks the build before it starts a session, and tells you to update if it is too old.

***

## Install an agent

When an agent is not installed, its row in **Settings → Agents** offers **Install**, which opens **Set up *agent***. Pick an install method, and Kepler runs the install command for you and shows its output. **Cancel** stops an install in progress. Once the install finishes, Kepler opens **Sign in to *agent*** if the agent needs a sign-in. Installs and updates run one at a time.

The install methods depend on the operating system of the machine you are on:

| Agent | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, winget, npm (global) |
| **Codex** | Standalone installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Standalone installer, npm (global) | Standalone installer, npm (global) |
| **GitHub Copilot** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | winget, npm (global) |
| **Cursor CLI** | Native installer, Homebrew | Native installer | Native installer |
| **Auggie** | npm (global) | npm (global) | npm (global) |
| **OpenCode** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global), pacman | npm (global) |
| **Grok Build** | Native installer | Native installer | Native installer |
| **Pi** | Native installer, npm (global) | Native installer, npm (global) | Native installer, npm (global) |
| **Google Antigravity** | Native installer | Native installer | Native installer |

Every OpenCode method installs OpenCode 2.

The dialog marks Claude Code's **npm (global)** method *Deprecated by Anthropic*.

Kepler offers a method only when the tool it runs is installed. For example, the Homebrew method needs Homebrew. A method that needs Node.js says so when Node.js is missing. If none of an agent's methods can run, Kepler says so and points you to the custom binary path instead.

**Kepler can run the copy that came with a desktop app.** When an agent's command-line tool is not installed but the vendor's desktop app is, such as Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, or OpenCode Desktop, Kepler runs the app's copy of the agent. The agent's page marks it **Desktop app**, and that copy updates only when the app does. To get a copy that updates itself, click **Install CLI** on the agent's page. Kepler then runs the standalone CLI instead. If the desktop app keeps its sign-in to itself, sign in to the agent once in Kepler.

If you already installed the agent somewhere Kepler did not find it, tell Kepler where it is from the same dialog:

1. Under **Already installed?**, type the program's full path in the **Full path to *agent*** field, or click **Browse…** to pick it.
2. Click **Use this**, or press **Enter**.

Kepler saves the path under **Which *agent* Kepler runs** if the agent runs from it. If it does not, Kepler keeps the path you had before.

The install output pane stays open after the install finishes. Read it before you dismiss it: errors such as a permissions failure appear only there.

***

## Binary detection

Kepler finds each agent's binary the way your shell does: the first match on your `PATH`, the same one `which` reports. It also finds an agent installed by nvm or Homebrew, even when you did not launch Kepler from a terminal. After you change your shell's startup files, click **Restart agent** or **Rescan**, and the agent picks up the change without a Kepler restart.

Each agent's page in **Settings → Agents** shows what Kepler resolved. Its version and **Install** sit beside the agent's name, and the program and its data folder have their own fields:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Version | The installed version, or **Not installed** |
| **Install** | Runs one of the install methods above. Shown when the agent is not installed |
| **Which *agent* Kepler runs** | The resolved absolute path, or **Not found**, with where it came from (**PATH**, **Shell**, **Common**, or **Desktop app**) and its version |
| **Rescan** | Re-detects this agent's binary. Use it after installing or removing one outside Kepler |
| **Custom path…** | Pins an absolute path of your own, which must be a file |
| **Clear custom** | Drops the pinned path and goes back to automatic resolution. Shown only while a custom path is set |
| **Installed versions** | A picker listing every install Kepler found, with an **Auto** row. Appears only when Kepler finds more than one |
| **Where *agent* keeps its data** | Overrides the agent's own data and config folder. Leave it empty for the agent's usual folder |
| The on/off switch | Whether Kepler offers this agent when you start a session. Also on the agent's row |

If Kepler cannot read an installed agent's version, its row shows a **Version unknown** badge, and features that depend on the version stay off, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. To fix it, reinstall or update the agent.

When an installed version has a known problem, the agent's page shows a warning under its name that says what to do. For example:

| Agent | What the warning tells you |
|---|---|
| **OpenCode** | OpenCode 1 is not supported, and its sessions do not start. Install OpenCode 2, or pick an OpenCode 2 binary |
| **Auggie** | **Auggie integration is unverified**: Kepler could not verify the selected build. Click **Rescan** or select a verified installation before you rely on MCP tools in Chat |
| **Codex** | This version can show approval prompts that need no answer. Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

If a custom path later disappears, such as after an auto-update removes an old version, Kepler finds the agent itself again instead of reporting it missing.

Beside the **Your agents** heading in **Settings → Agents**, **Rescan** re-detects every agent at once, and **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater. A row shows **Update available** when a newer version of that agent is out.

***

## Sign in to an agent

An installed agent shows **Sign in** until it has a credential, and **Sign out** once it does. **Sign in** opens a modal listing the methods that agent supports on this machine, plus any methods Kepler provides itself. If the agent refuses a credential, the account shows **Sign in** again, and the modal shows the agent's reason:

| Agent | How you sign in |
|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Browser sign-in. Kepler runs the sign-in for you and your browser opens; you paste a code back only if the browser callback cannot reach Kepler. **More sign-in options** adds **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, **Microsoft Foundry**, and **LLM gateway** |
| **Codex** | Sign in with a ChatGPT account through your browser, or enter an API key. On a remote, **ChatGPT (device code)** |
| **GitHub Copilot** | **Sign in with GitHub**: open `github.com/login/device` and enter the one-time code Kepler shows |
| **Cursor CLI** | Cursor's own browser sign-in, driven from the modal, or **Paste an API key** from the Cursor dashboard. On a remote, only the API key works |
| **Auggie** | **Sign in with browser**, or **Paste session token** |
| **OpenCode** | **OpenCode account (Go or Console)**: sign in through your browser with a one-time code. OpenCode also resolves providers from its own config file and provider environment variables |
| **Grok Build** | Browser sign-in, or **Paste an API key** for a deployment with no local browser |
| **Google Antigravity** | **Sign in in Terminal**: sign in, type `/exit` in the terminal, then confirm in the modal. The modal also lists the Google sign-in methods the CLI offers |
| **Pi** | Nothing to do in Kepler. Sign in inside the CLI itself, or set the provider environment variables it reads |

### Claude Code through a cloud provider or gateway

To run Claude Code through your cloud provider rather than a Claude account, click **More sign-in options** in the **Sign in to Claude Code** modal and pick a method:

| Method | What you enter |
|---|---|
| **Amazon Bedrock** | A Bedrock API key (`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`) and the AWS region (`AWS_REGION`) |
| **Google Vertex AI** | The project (`ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID`) and region (`CLOUD_ML_REGION`), and optionally a credentials file (`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`). Leave the file empty to use application default credentials |
| **Microsoft Foundry** | The resource name only (`ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE`), and optionally an API key and your Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku deployment names. Without a key, it signs in with Microsoft Entra ID credentials on this machine |
| **LLM gateway** | The gateway's URL (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`) and the token it issues (`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`), plus any other `NAME=value` variables your gateway needs |

The account then reads as the provider and its region, project, or resource, or as the gateway's host. Kepler shows no plan usage for it, because the plan belongs to your cloud provider. Saving one method clears the values stored for the others, and **Sign out** clears the provider. You can set a gateway's extra variables only on the computer running Kepler, not from a paired device.

### OpenCode account

**OpenCode account (Go or Console)** signs OpenCode in to your OpenCode account:

1. Click **Sign in** on OpenCode's row and pick **OpenCode account (Go or Console)**.
2. Click **Open sign-in in browser** and enter the **One-time code** the modal shows.
3. Choose the workspace with your Go subscription.
4. Select a Go model to use your plan.

OpenCode's row then shows it as signed in.

### Browser sign-in, including on a remote

**Claude Code** and **Codex** both sign in through your browser, and neither needs a terminal to do it.

This also works on a [remote environment](/kepler/remote-environments):

- **Claude Code** on a remote offers **Sign in with Claude.ai**, which opens Claude's sign-in in your *local* browser and takes the code you paste back. Kepler saves the credential on the remote machine. **Sign in with token (advanced)** is for an account that cannot finish a browser sign-in.
- **Codex** on a remote offers **ChatGPT (device code)**. Kepler shows the sign-in link and a **One-time code**, and the credential is saved on the remote machine. Some ChatGPT workspaces turn device sign-in off, and Kepler then points you to the alternatives.
- **Cursor CLI** on a remote offers only **Paste an API key**, because its browser sign-in cannot complete there.

Wherever Kepler opens a browser sign-in for Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity, **Open sign-in in browser** appears beside a read-only **Sign-in link** field with **Copy link**. To open the link in another browser or profile, copy it.

When a sign-in runs in a terminal on a remote and the browser page does not load after you sign in, paste that page's address into the box under the terminal and click **Send**. Kepler opens the address on the remote machine, if the sign-in printed it. You then finish in the terminal.

**Import local Codex login** is the other remote route, in the desktop app: it copies this machine's `~/.codex/auth.json` to the remote target, and asks you to confirm on this machine before it reads the file. The import copies a credential: anyone with access to that remote machine can send Codex requests on your account until you sign out.

A Codex API key that you enter in the modal works both locally and on a remote. **Sign out** on Codex signs the CLI itself out, and Kepler follows a sign-in you do in the Codex CLI outside Kepler.

### Auggie's sign-in methods

Auggie supports 2 sign-in methods:

| Method | What it does | Where it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Sign in with browser** | Runs Auggie's sign-in and finishes it in your browser | Local, and over SSH: the remote variant opens the page in your local browser and takes a pasted JSON response |
| **Paste session token** | You paste the JSON from `auggie token print` into Kepler. Kepler stores it and supplies it on every session | Anywhere, including CI-style setups with no browser |

If you run Auggie's browser sign-in on this machine yourself, Kepler detects it and you can skip the token paste.

### Multiple accounts of one agent

**Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Auggie**, and **Grok Build** support more than one signed-in account. To add one, click **Add account** on the agent's row in **Settings → Agents**, or under **Accounts** on the agent's page. Each account keeps its own credentials. Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot accounts can share their conversation history with the CLI, and a Copilot account shares it by default.

To give each added account its own color, pick one from the swatch at the left of its row. Kepler tints the agent icon with that color on session tabs, the task's context panel, and the terminal status bar, so you can tell sessions on different accounts apart. The default account stays uncolored.

For **Auggie**, you can only add a second account with **Paste session token**. Its browser sign-in would sign the second account in as the first.

***

## Run modes

Every agent except Pi runs in 2 modes. To pick the mode new sessions start in for every agent, set **New sessions start in** under **Settings → Agents → Defaults**. To give one agent its own mode, click its row and set **New sessions start in** on its page:

| Mode | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Chat** | Kepler shows the conversation itself, with replies, diffs, and plans you can read, review, and search. This is the default |
| **Terminal** | The agent's own command-line app, with its commands, shortcuts, and settings, in a terminal inside the task |

To start one session in the other mode without changing the default, use the Chat and Terminal switch at the composer's input before you send the first message. An agent that offers only one mode shows no switch at all. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

Chat sessions show up as Kepler in places such as your Anthropic dashboard.

### Detecting sessions started outside Kepler

**Settings → General → Sessions outside Kepler → Show them in Kepler** is a separate setting that applies to all agents, and it is **on by default**. It installs GitKraken hooks so sessions you start in your own terminal show up in Kepler. It covers every agent Kepler can track that way: **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Cursor**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, **Grok Build**, **Pi**, and **Google Antigravity**. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

Kepler also follows its own **Terminal** sessions this way. If a running Terminal session stops reporting to Kepler, Kepler warns that **Agent sessions aren't reporting to Kepler**. Click **Repair**, then restart any session that still does not report. To repair sessions running on another computer, use Kepler on that computer.

### Programs that report their own status

Some terminal programs report their own status to Kepler. When an agent's terminal program does this, Kepler shows the session as working, blocked, or done from what the program reports. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#whats-different-in-terminal).

***

## Your default agent

**New sessions start with**, in **Settings → Agents → Defaults**, sets the agent, account, model, mode, and options a new session starts with. You pick them in the same **Agent settings** pill as the composer, and you can start from an [agent preset](/kepler/settings-agents#agent-presets). **Start each session on the agent you used last** is on by default: your first session uses the pill's agent, and each later one starts on your last pick. To always start on the pill's agent, clear it. See [Defaults](/kepler/settings-agents#defaults).

Kepler saves agent options **per account**. Picking a different account of the same agent brings up that account's own saved model and options, so a larger model you chose on your work account does not carry over to your personal one.

Only agents that are installed and switched on appear in the picker. If your saved default is no longer installed, Kepler says so and asks you to pick another.

An Action can override all of this. See [Actions](/kepler/actions) for how an Action pins a provider, account, model, mode, and options together, and which choice wins when they disagree.

***

## Custom agents

If your agent is not one of the 9 supported agents, you can add it by its command. To add one, open **Settings → Agents → Custom agents**, click **New custom agent**, and fill in these fields:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Name** | What the agent is called in Kepler's pickers |
| **Runs in** | **Chat** (Kepler's chat, for a program that speaks ACP) or **Terminal** (the command's own app, in a terminal) |
| **Command** | The binary to run: an absolute path, or a name Kepler resolves on your `PATH` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments for the command. For a Chat agent, the arguments that put it into ACP mode, for example `--acp` |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Variables merged into the agent's environment on every session |

Kepler treats environment values as secrets: it encrypts them at rest and hides them after you save. When you edit a custom agent, leaving a value empty (`KEY=`) keeps the stored secret, and typing a new value replaces it.

Custom agents appear alongside the built-in agents everywhere you can choose an agent. A custom agent that runs in **Terminal** works the same way as a built-in one.

***

## MCP servers

Kepler lists the MCP servers each agent loads. You can add, remove, sign in to, and turn off servers or single tools, for one session from the composer's **Agent settings** pill, per repository, or as defaults in **Settings → Agent tools → MCP servers**. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

***

## Sessions

After you connect an agent, you run it in a **session** inside a task. To learn how to start and resume sessions, queue prompts, and review what the agent produced, see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

A task holds resources and does not require a worktree, or even a repository. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

To follow conversations you started outside Kepler, see [Sessions started outside Kepler](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

---

---
# MCP Servers
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/mcp-servers/
product: Kepler
feature: MCP Servers
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Your coding agents load **Model Context Protocol** (**MCP**) servers from their own config files. Kepler reads those files and lists exactly the servers each agent loads. From Kepler, without editing the agent's config by hand, you can:

- See the servers each agent loads.
- Turn a server, or one of its tools, off where you do not want it.
- Add or remove a server.
- Sign in to a server that needs it.

You manage MCP servers for one session, per repository, or as global defaults. See [Where you manage them](#where-you-manage-them).

## Requirements and limits

- Works for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Cursor**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, and **Grok Build**. Pi, Antigravity, and custom agents do not expose their MCP servers to Kepler.
- The agent must be installed. Settings lists only the agents that answer.
- Kepler shows the servers the agent's config files define. Kepler does not list servers that are not stored on disk, such as claude.ai connectors.

***

## Where you manage them

| Where | What a change applies to |
|---|---|
| The composer's **Agent settings** pill → **MCP servers** → **Manage** | That session, or the session the **New task** composer starts. For Cursor and Grok Build, this repository |
| **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers** | This repository, for the agent you pick |
| **Settings → Agent tools → MCP servers** | Every repository, as the default each one inherits |

The **MCP servers** dialog in the composer has **Repo settings** in its header, which opens the same list in **Settings → Repositories**.

Every place shows the same manager. It groups servers by where they apply:

| Group | Where the server comes from |
|---|---|
| **All repos** | Your own config for the agent, used in every repository |
| **This repo · Shared with your team** | Checked into this repository |
| **This repo · Only you** | This repository only, not shared |
| **From plugins** | Installed by a plugin |
| **From your organization** | Managed by your organization |

Each row is a server. The switch on a row turns the server on or off, and clicking the row opens the server's own page. A row can carry these badges:

- **Sign in needed**: the server needs authentication before the agent can use it.
- **Switch affects all repos**: turning the server on or off here changes it in every repository.
- **Locked**: Kepler cannot edit the server's entry in the agent's config file, such as a server your organization manages.

***

<a id="per-session"></a>

## For one session

To switch servers for one session:

1. In a session or in the **New task** composer, open the **Agent settings** pill.
2. In the **MCP servers** row, click **Manage**. The **MCP servers** dialog opens.

When you open a server's page, **All servers** takes you back to the list.

For Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot, turning a server on or off here applies to that session only, or to the session the **New task** composer starts. Your repository and global defaults stay as they are. To reuse the choice, click **Save preset**: the [agent preset](/kepler/settings-agents#agent-presets) keeps it.

A session cannot turn on a server that is off in the agent's own settings. To use it, turn it on in Settings first.

Turning off a single tool from the dialog still changes it for the repository. For Cursor and Grok Build, every switch in the dialog changes the repository.

***

## Per repository

To set the servers for every session in one repository, open **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers**, or click **Repo settings** in the composer's **MCP servers** dialog. A change here applies to that repository and all of its worktrees.

If a server is off in Settings and you have not turned it on for the repository, the server's row says so, with **Open Settings** to go to the global default. Turning it on here turns it on for this repository only.

### Turn off a single tool

A server's page lists its **Tools** under the **Let *agent* use this server** switch. If the server needs authentication, sign in to it to see its tools.

To keep the agent from calling one tool, open the server's page and turn off the tool's switch.

Turning off a single tool works for Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build. For the other agents, turn the whole server off instead.

***

## Global defaults

**Settings → Agent tools → MCP servers** is the same manager with no repository. Use the **Agent** picker at the top to choose the agent, and the account when that agent has more than one.

**Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent**, on by default, gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn it off to manage that server yourself.

The repository and global levels combine like this:

- A repository uses the global value until you change that server for it in **Settings → Repositories**, or, for Cursor and Grok Build, in the composer's dialog.
- A repository's choice wins over the global one, in either direction: a repository can turn off a server that's on globally, or turn on a server that's off globally.
- Switching a server back to match the global default makes it follow the default again.

You cannot change plugin servers or Cursor servers in Settings, although plugin servers are listed there. Cursor keeps its on and off state per project, so switch a Cursor server from a repository's dialog instead.

***

## Add and remove servers

To add a server, click **Add server**: beside the section's heading in Settings, or at the foot of the list in the MCP servers dialog. The **Add MCP server (*agent*)** page opens with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, or `-`, up to 64 characters, unique where it is saved |
| **Applies to** | **All repos**, **This repo · Only you**, or **This repo · Shared with your team**. The choices depend on the agent and on whether you are in a repository, and the field shows only when there is more than 1 choice, as in a repository's **MCP servers** section |
| **Runs as** | **Command** for a local server, or **URL** or **URL (SSE)** for a remote one |
| **Command** and **Arguments** | For a command server, for example `npx -y @some/server` |
| **URL** | For a remote server, an `http://` or `https://` address |
| **Environment variables** / **Headers** | Key and value pairs. Values stay hidden until you choose **Show value** |

Kepler writes the new server into the agent's own config file, in the format that agent uses, so the agent's CLI sees it too.

To remove a server, open the server's page and click **Remove server**. Kepler deletes the server from the agent's config. You cannot undo this.

You cannot remove these servers from Kepler:

- Plugin servers.
- Managed servers.
- GitHub Copilot servers defined in a repository. You can remove only the Copilot servers in your own config.

***

## Copy a server to other agents

To use a server you already set up with another agent or account, copy it instead of adding it again. Kepler copies the server's full definition, including its environment variables and headers.

1. Open the server's page.
2. Click **Also add to…**.
3. Select each agent, or each account of an agent, that should get the server.
4. Click **Add to *N* destinations**.

If one copy fails, the others still go ahead, and the failed destination stays selected with its error.

You cannot copy servers from plugins, so their page does not show **Also add to…**.

***

## Sign in to a server

For a server that needs authentication, its page has a **Sign-in** section. It offers **Sign in**, or **Re-authenticate** once you are signed in, and **Clear authentication** to sign the server out. Kepler signs in under the same account the session uses, and the agent uses that sign-in outside Kepler too. Sign-in is available for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor servers.

In a local window, **Open sign-in page** opens your browser, and Kepler finishes when you are done. In a window connected to a remote environment, sign in on that page, then paste the URL you land on into **Redirect URL**.

If your organization manages the agent's settings, sign-in first lists them for your approval. Click **Approve and continue** to sign in, or **Decline** if you do not recognize them. Kepler saves your approval for this account.

***

## When changes apply

| Where the change lands | When it takes effect |
|---|---|
| A Claude Code **Chat** session | Right away. The session keeps its conversation, model, and mode |
| A terminal session, or any other agent's session | On restart. The **Agent settings** pill and the dialog show how many MCP changes are waiting, with **Restart agent** |
| The **New task** composer | The session you start comes up with that state |

Whether an on or off choice also reaches the agent's own CLI depends on the agent:

- **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot**: Kepler does not edit the agent's config, so the same agent run from your own terminal is not affected. The one exception is turning on a Claude Code server that Claude's own config lists as disabled: Kepler can do this only by editing that list.
- **Cursor and Grok Build**: Kepler writes the change into the agent's own files, which their CLIs also read.
- **Auggie**: Kepler lists the servers without a switch, because Auggie has no way to turn a server off. To stop using a server, edit Auggie's config.

Adding and removing a server always edits the config file.

Each agent account keeps its own MCP setup. Other Claude Code accounts start with the default account's servers.

***

## Related

- [Agent Tool Settings](/kepler/settings-agent-tools#mcp-servers): **Settings → Agent tools**, including the **MCP servers** section.
- [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations): the agents Kepler runs and how to set them up.
- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions): the composer's **Agent settings** pill, and restarting a session.

---

---
# Issue Tracker Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Issue Tracker Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Connect an issue tracker to see the issues you are working on in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface), alongside your pull requests and the tasks you already have running. To start work on an issue, you pick its row instead of describing the work from scratch.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

***

## Trackers Kepler can read issues from

Of Kepler's 13 providers, 11 return issues:

| Provider | Also returns pull requests |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Jira** | No |
| **Jira Server / Data Center** | No |
| **Linear** | No |
| **Trello** | No |
| **Asana** | No |

Jira, Linear, Trello, and Asana do not appear in pull-request filters.

The other 2 providers, **Bitbucket** and **Bitbucket Data Center**, return pull requests only. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** read issues the same way their cloud counterparts do. Which fields come back depends on your server's version, and your machine needs to be able to reach the server. You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted tracker](#connect-a-self-hosted-tracker).

Kepler trusts the certificates installed in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority, or a network that re-signs HTTPS traffic, works without extra setup.

***

## Connect a tracker

To connect a cloud tracker (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Azure DevOps**, **Jira**, **Linear**, **Trello**, or **Asana**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler on GitKraken's website, which opens in your browser.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. The exception is a self-hosted connection you keep on this device only. See [Connect a self-hosted tracker](#connect-a-self-hosted-tracker). To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account. Kepler prompts you if you are not signed in.

If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog Kepler shows while you authorize, and open it in a browser yourself. Each link works once, so **Try again** makes a new one. The dialog closes by itself once the connection appears.

### Connect a self-hosted tracker

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect *provider*** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the issues you need.
5. To keep the server URL and the token on this device, tick **Keep PAT on this device only**. Kepler then never sends them to GitKraken, and the connection is not available on your other devices or in other GitKraken products.
6. Click **Save connection**.

Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine and saves it on this device. Unless you kept it on this device only, Kepler also adds the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports one of these results:

- The server accepted the token.
- Kepler saved the token without being able to reach the server or verify its certificate.
- The server refused the token. Check its value and permissions.

For every message the dialog shows, see [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**.

Once connected, a self-hosted provider lists each server on its own row, with a storage chip, **Set as primary**, **Replace PAT**, and **Disconnect**. Each server keeps its own repositories and issues:

- To connect another server, click **Add connection** on the provider's row.
- To renew an expired or rejected token, click **Replace PAT** on that server's row.
- To move a server's token between your GitKraken account and this device, click its storage chip (**GitKraken account** or **This device only**) and choose **Keep PAT on this device only** or **Store PAT in GitKraken account**. A connection kept on this device only cannot be set as primary.
- To make a server the provider's default connection, click **Set as primary**. Agents' GitKraken MCP server acts through the primary connection.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider's primary connection. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can also show a warning:

| Warning | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Sign-in expired** | The provider's sign-in has expired | Wait for Kepler to refresh it, or click **Reconnect** |
| **Cannot connect to server** | Kepler could not reach the server; the integration is still connected | Check that the server is reachable from your network or VPN; the warning clears on its own |
| **Unexpected response** | Kepler could not read the provider's answer, so some items may be missing | Reconnecting does not help; if it stays, check for a proxy or gateway between Kepler and the provider |
| An organization named under the row | That organization refuses Kepler's access, so only its items are left out | Follow the row's advice, such as **Request access on GitHub** |

You do not have to open Settings to find a failing provider. Todo, the **Resources** screen's lists, and a link preview name it too, with the one fix that applies: **Reconnect**, **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, **Open settings**, or **Retry**. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#where-your-pull-requests-turn-up) for each warning.

***

## Choose what Kepler brings in

Each connected integration except Trello and Asana has a visibility line under its row in **Settings → Integrations**. The line reads **Everything visible**, or how many items you have hidden.

To hide part of an integration:

1. Click **Choose what's visible…** on the provider's row. The **Choose what *provider* brings in** dialog opens.
2. Clear the checkbox of each item to hide. Type in **Filter…** to narrow a long list.
3. Click **Save**.

What the dialog lists depends on the provider:

| Provider | Lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | **Organizations** and **Repositories** |
| **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | **Organizations**, **Repositories**, and **Projects** |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear** | **Projects** |

A ticked item is visible. Hiding an organization also hides its repositories, which show *Hidden with its organization* and cannot be ticked on their own. A hidden project leaves the issue lists but stays in the project pickers. A project that has not returned any issues yet may be missing from the dialog's list.

Hidden items are left out of Todo, the issue and pull request lists, and the pickers. Tasks and branches already linked to a hidden item keep working. Kepler saves the choice on your GitKraken account, so it follows you to other machines where you sign in.

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider: two GitHub accounts, a work Jira site and a personal one. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's issues and pull requests from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary as it is. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

**Agents keep acting as the primary account.** Your agents' GitKraken MCP server always uses the primary connection of your GitKraken account, even when Kepler reads a provider through another account.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters.

**Reconnect keeps your choices.** When one account's sign-in fails, **Reconnect** renews that account's connection and keeps your primary and read choices.

The read account also authenticates Git. When you start work on an issue in a repository you have never cloned, Kepler clones that repository with the same connection it reads through. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations) for which hosts this covers and what happens on the hosts it does not.

**Linear connections stay separate by workspace.** Each Linear account's entry shows the Linear workspace it was granted. Connections to different workspaces are separate accounts, each reading only its own workspace's issues.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely, with its saved filters and its rows in your lists.

Disconnecting a self-hosted server whose token is kept on this device only removes the token from this device alone. Your GitKraken account and your other devices are not affected.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## What Kepler reads from an issue

When an issue becomes a task, Kepler attaches what it read, so the agent starts with that context instead of asking for it. Kepler reads these fields from the issue:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Identifier** | The issue key or number: `GK-1234` for Jira, `DRE-2` for Linear, a number for GitHub, GitLab, and Azure DevOps |
| **Title** | |
| **Description** | The issue body, or an Azure DevOps field such as **Repro Steps** on a Bug, labeled with its name |
| **Issue type** | The provider's own type, such as a Jira issue type |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one |
| **Assignees** | |
| **Status** | The issue's current state, in the provider's own words, such as Jira's *To Verify* |
| **Last updated** | When the issue was last updated |
| **Labels** | The provider's own labels, shown as badges in issue previews |
| **Project or board** | Jira projects, Linear teams, Azure DevOps areas. Git hosts attach issues to a repository instead |
| **Iteration or sprint** | Azure DevOps iterations and Jira sprints. A Jira issue carried across sprints keeps them all |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host, for the git hosts |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Jira**, and so on |

Kepler does not read an issue's priority field, due date, Trello checklist, or Linear cycle. An agent can still find these by opening the issue's URL itself, but Kepler does not deliver them as attached context.

Kepler reads an issue's milestone on GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab Self-Hosted, and Linear, so Todo can group and filter by **Milestone**. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

Todo's **Priority** grouping and filter come from labels instead: a label such as `P1`, `priority: high`, `blocker`, or `critical` sets the level, and the most urgent label wins. Jira and Linear keep priority in a field Kepler does not read, so their issues show as **Unprioritised** unless a label sets a priority. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

Jira and Azure DevOps descriptions keep their headings, code blocks, and tables in Kepler's previews and in the agent's context.

Images embedded in an issue's description, including Jira and Azure DevOps attachments, display in Kepler's issue previews, from self-hosted servers too. The agent receives the description as text: Kepler does not pass the attachments or images themselves.

### Comments

When you open an issue in a reader, either the task panel's side pane or the issue's pane on the task page, a **Comments** section under the summary shows its discussion. Kepler reads comments for **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Jira**, and **Jira Server / Data Center**. For other providers, the section says that comments for that provider are not available in Kepler yet.

Kepler shows up to the newest 100 comments, newest at the bottom. **Show earlier comments** shows older ones, and **Refresh comments** reads the discussion again. Comments are for you to read: Kepler does not attach them to the task or pass them to the agent.

### Which issues Kepler lists

Kepler lists open work. An issue that is finished or canceled in its tracker (a Linear issue in *Done* or *Canceled*, for example) leaves **Todo** and the issue pickers. An issue already attached to a task keeps showing on that task with its real state, finished or not.

A Todo view has 2 scopes, set in its **View** menu under **Scope**:

- **Mine**: the issues related to you, across every organization you belong to.
- **All**: also adds the open issues of the repositories added to Kepler on GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, and GitLab Self-Hosted. On other providers, it lists the same issues as **Mine**.

Under **All**, **Repos** and **Updated** narrow the view by repository and by how recently each issue was updated. **All repos in Kepler** skips a very large repository and says so, with **Choose repos** to add it anyway.

Under **Mine**, each provider reports a different set of issues related to you:

| Provider | Issues Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or mentioning you |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Yours or assigned to you |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear**, **Trello**, **Asana** | Assigned to you |

An issue listed only because you were mentioned is marked **Mentioned**, so you can tell it apart from work that is yours. Under **All**, the **Your role** filter also offers **Not mine**.

To find issues to add to a task, the issue list on a task's **Resources** screen has its own scope menu: **Related to me**, **All in my repos** (the open issues in the repositories added to Kepler), or **All visible**.

For GitHub and Azure DevOps, **All visible** reads every issue across your organizations, including repositories you can read outside them, such as ones where you are an outside collaborator. It loads more slowly. Jira and Linear show only your issues there until you pick a project or a team:

- **Jira**: when the issue list shows Jira alone, a project picker appears, starting with **All projects**. Pick a project to see every open issue in it. Kepler remembers the pick for each Jira connection.
- **Linear**: when the issue list shows Linear alone, a team picker and a **Project** picker appear. Pick a team, a Linear project, or both, to see every open issue in them, whoever it is assigned to. The **Project** picker lists your Linear workspace's projects with their state, closed ones included.
