**A Linear issue synced with GitHub shows once.** When Linear's GitHub Issues sync keeps a two-way copy of a Linear issue on GitHub, Kepler lists the pair as one row, the Linear issue. The pair shares one task history, so a task started from either copy is the issue's task. Pairing works for GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

When you start work from the Linear issue, Kepler uses the repository of its GitHub copy if exactly one repository you have in Kepler matches it.

***

## Where your issues turn up

Your issues appear in 3 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | A **Todo** view lists your issues across every connected tracker, grouped and filtered how you like |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button on a row hands the issue to an agent with its context attached. Running an Action on an issue that has no task also turns it into a task |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | An issue is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

The **Issue type**, **Label**, **Project**, and **Status** filters use your provider's own terms, not Kepler's. Azure DevOps and Jira issues also filter by **Iteration** and **Sprint**, each named the way its tracker names it.

Kepler recognizes an issue from its URL when you paste or attach one, including these work item URLs:

- **GitLab** work items, at `/-/work_items/<number>` in a project. A group-level work item stays a plain link.
- **Azure DevOps** work items, at `/<organization>/<project>/_workitems/edit/<number>` or at the organization level, `/<organization>/_workitems/edit/<number>`.

**Search by key or link.** In the issue list of a task's **Resources** screen, type a Jira or Linear issue key, such as `OPS-42`, or paste a Jira Cloud, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, or Azure DevOps work item link. Kepler finds that issue in its tracker, whatever its state, even when it is not in the list. A Jira Server / Data Center link resolves when it points at an installation you have connected.

**Jira keys in commits and branches.** With Jira or Jira Server / Data Center connected, Kepler links Jira issue keys in commit messages and branch names, so `OPS-42` in a commit message links to that issue. Right-click a commit in a worktree's commit list for **Open issue *key*** and **Copy issue URL for *key*** (see [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes#the-changes-panel)), and the **Worktrees and branches** page shows the keys as chips on branch and worktree rows (see [Repository Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#worktrees-and-branches)). Only Jira keys are linked this way.

**Add from the list with the keyboard.** In the issue list on the **Resources** screen, the arrows move between rows, and **Space** or **Enter** ticks the row. Ticked issues go onto the task when you click **Save changes**. **Show preview** in the screen's header shows the focused row beside the list. See [Picking issues and pull requests](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#picking-issues-and-pull-requests).

**Paste a link on the Links tab.** An issue URL pasted on the **Links** tab of the **Resources** screen is looked up and added as that issue, with **Add as plain link** to keep it a plain link. See [Pasting an issue link](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#pasting-an-issue-link).

**Paste a link into a prompt.** Paste an issue or pull request URL into a session's or a new task's composer and it becomes a link chip, which Kepler attaches to the task when you send. See [Sending a prompt](/kepler/agent-sessions#sending-a-prompt).

### Close, reopen, or delete a GitHub issue

You can change a GitHub.com issue's state without leaving Kepler. Click **Manage GitHub issue**, the pencil after the issue's title in its panel header or side-pane reader, or open the menu on a linked issue's card:

- **Close issue** asks for a **Closing reason**: **Completed** or **Not planned**.
- **Reopen issue** opens a closed issue again.
- **Delete issue** removes the issue from GitHub for everyone, after you confirm. A deleted issue reads **Deleted** in Kepler.

Closing keeps the discussion and lets you reopen the issue later, so close an issue unless you need it gone.

An agent can change GitHub issues too, and deleting one always asks you first. See [What an agent can do with a task's resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#repositories-and-actions).

---

---
# Pull Request Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/pull-request-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Pull Request Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Connect a Git host to see the pull requests you authored, and the ones waiting on your review, in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). Kepler also matches each pull request to your existing worktrees, so a branch you are working on shows its pull request wherever the branch appears.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

Each connected Git host has a visibility line under its row. The line reads **Everything visible**, or shows how many items you have hidden. To leave organizations or repositories out of Todo, the lists, and the pickers, click **Choose what's visible…**. See [Choose what Kepler brings in](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#choose-what-kepler-brings-in).

***

## Hosts Kepler can read pull requests from

Of Kepler's 13 providers, 8 return pull requests:

| Provider | Also returns issues |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Bitbucket** | No |
| **Bitbucket Data Center** | No |

Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center do not appear in issue filters.

The other 5 providers (Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, Trello, and Asana) return issues only. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** read pull requests and merge requests the same way their cloud counterparts do. Which fields come back depends on your server's version.

You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted instance](#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). Your machine needs to be able to reach the server. Kepler trusts the certificates in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority works without extra setup.

Kepler shows GitLab merge requests as pull requests, in the same list.

***

## Connect a Git host

To connect a cloud Git host (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Bitbucket**, or **Azure DevOps**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler on GitKraken's website, which opens in your browser.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account.

If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog Kepler shows while you authorize, and open it in a browser yourself. Each link works once, so **Try again** makes a new one. The dialog closes by itself once the connection appears. **Reconnect** uses the same dialog.

### Connect a self-hosted instance

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect *provider*** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the repositories you need.
5. To keep the server URL and the token on this device, tick **Keep PAT on this device only**. Kepler then never sends them to GitKraken, and the connection is not available on your other devices or in other GitKraken products.
6. Click **Save connection**.

The address must be `http` or `https`, without credentials, a query, or a fragment. Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine and saves it on this device. Unless you kept it on this device only, Kepler also adds the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports how the check went:

| Message | What it means |
|---|---|
| *Credentials verified with the server.* | The server accepted the token |
| *Credentials saved. Unable to verify the server certificate. Check its TLS configuration.* | Kepler saved the token but could not verify the server's certificate |
| *Credentials saved without verification. Unable to reach the server.* | Kepler saved the token without checking it |
| *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.* | Fix the token and save again |

Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**, and you cannot make that connection the primary. If Kepler cannot reach GitKraken, it retries when you refresh your providers.

Once connected, a self-hosted provider lists each server on its own row, with a storage chip, **Set as primary**, **Replace PAT**, and **Disconnect**. Each server keeps its own repositories and pull requests:

- To connect another server, click **Add connection** on the provider's row.
- To renew an expired or rejected token, click **Replace PAT** on that server's row.
- To move a server's token between your GitKraken account and this device, click its storage chip (**GitKraken account** or **This device only**) and choose **Keep PAT on this device only** or **Store PAT in GitKraken account**. A connection kept on this device only cannot be set as primary.
- To make a server the provider's default connection, click **Set as primary**.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can show a warning:

- **Sign-in expired**: the token needs refreshing. Kepler tries to refresh it by itself; **Reconnect** refreshes it by hand.
- **Cannot connect to server**: the integration is still connected, but Kepler could not reach the server. Instead of reconnecting, check that the server is up and reachable from your network or VPN.
- An organization named under the row: that organization refuses Kepler's access, such as a GitHub organization that restricts OAuth apps. Kepler leaves out only that organization's items.

See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) for the warnings in full.

***

## Cloning a repository for a pull request

When you start work on a pull request from a repository you have never cloned, Kepler first clones the repository into your **Repositories folder** (**Settings → Repositories**). How the clone signs in depends on the host:

| Host | How the clone authenticates |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Your connected account's token |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Your connected account's token |
| **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Your own Git credentials |

A self-hosted repository clones through the account connected to that server. When a provider has more than one account, the clone uses the account Kepler reads from: **Read from this account** where you set one, otherwise the primary.

Kepler does not write the token into the clone's `.git/config` or the remote's URL.

If Kepler has no usable token for the host, the clone uses your own Git credential helper. Kepler cannot prompt you for Git credentials, so with no credential helper the clone fails. To fix it, sign in with a Git credential helper (for example, `gh auth login`) or use an SSH URL, then try again.

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's pull requests and issues from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary alone. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

**Agents keep acting as the primary account.** Your agents' GitKraken MCP server always uses the primary connection of your GitKraken account, even when Kepler reads a provider through another account.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely, with its saved filters and its rows in your lists.

Disconnecting a self-hosted server whose token is kept on this device only removes the token from this device alone. Your GitKraken account and your other devices are not affected.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## How pull requests attach to worktrees

Kepler matches a pull request to a worktree by its branch, so a branch shows its pull request, even after the pull request merges.

### Auto-attaching a matched pull request

When you open a pull request outside Kepler (with `gh` in a terminal, from GitKraken Desktop, or on the web), Kepler attaches it to the task for you. The pull request then behaves like one you attached yourself: it appears in the task's resources, and the agent receives it as context. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

Kepler attaches only an open pull request that is yours, from a branch that matches a worktree's branch on an active task in the same repository. To link a teammate's pull request, attach it yourself.

Kepler never removes or replaces a link. Several active tasks can share one pull request.

***

## What Kepler reads from a pull request

Kepler reads these fields from a pull request:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Number and title** | |
| **Description** | The pull request body |
| **State** | **Open**, **Draft**, **Merged**, or **Closed** |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one. A row shows **Yours** for a pull request you authored, and **Review** for someone else's |
| **Head and base branch** | When the provider reports them |
| **Fork** | Whether the head branch lives on a fork, and where |
| **Created at** | |
| **Checks and review** | Shown on an open or draft pull request's chip in a task panel: failing, pending, or passing checks, and an approved review |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Bitbucket**, and so on |

A merged pull request keeps its description and author for as long as a task, archived or not, still links it.

Images embedded in a pull request's description display in Kepler's previews, including on GitHub Enterprise, GitLab Self-Hosted, and Azure DevOps Server.

***

## Where your pull requests turn up

Your pull requests appear in 4 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | A **Todo** view lists the pull requests related to you on each connected host, or every open one in the repositories added to Kepler |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button hands the pull request to an agent. **Review** and **Address Feedback** are the 2 built-in Actions for pull requests, and Kepler picks one based on who authored the pull request |
| [Review What a Coding Agent Changed](/kepler/review-changes) | Reading the diff and the commits behind a pull request |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | A pull request is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

**Todo's scope.** A Todo view's **View** menu sets its **Scope**: **Mine**, the work related to you, or **All**, which adds the open pull requests of the repositories added to Kepler on every Git host above. See [Which issues Kepler lists](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#which-issues-kepler-lists).

Under **Mine**, each provider reports a different set of pull requests related to you, so Todo lists these from each:

| Host | Pull requests Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or ones you review |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | Yours or awaiting your review |
| **Bitbucket** | Yours, or awaiting your review in your workspaces and repositories added to Kepler |

The pull request list on a task's **Resources** screen has its own scope menu: **Related to me** or **All in my repos**.

**Review requests come from every host.** Pull requests waiting on your review show up from every Git host above. On a large Bitbucket workspace, review requests can take a while to appear.

**Lists stay current while you look at them.** Pull request and issue lists refresh while they are on screen, and again when you come back to the window. When one provider fails to load, the others keep loading, and the failed provider's last loaded pull requests stay in the list.

**A failing provider is named, with its fix.** When a connected provider's read fails, Todo, the **Resources** screen's lists, and a link preview show a warning that names the provider and the fix, such as *Sign in to GitHub again to load its work.* Each warning offers one fix:

| What went wrong | The fix offered |
|---|---|
| The sign-in needs renewing | **Reconnect**, or **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, which needs a new token |
| The provider refused part of the request, so some organizations or repositories are missing | **Open settings** |
| Rate limiting, an unreachable server, an unreadable answer, or a temporary problem | **Retry** |

On Todo, each warning also has **Filter out *provider***, which hides that provider from the Todo view so it stops reporting the failure. To show the provider again, clear it in the view's **Provider** filter.

Rows kept from the last good load show a cloud mark on their provider chip.

**The pull request picker says why its list is empty.** When you add a pull request from the **Resources** screen, the picker explains an empty list:

- If the **Linked work** filter hides pull requests, the picker says how many it hides and which filter hides them, and offers **Show all**.
- If no connected provider can list pull requests, the picker reads **Connect your code host** and lists the providers that can fill the tab, each with **Connect**.

The **Linked work** filter defaults to **No active task**, which shows pull requests with no task or with archived tasks only. A task counts as active until you archive it, so Done and on-hold tasks count. To see every pull request, choose **Any**.

A row with task history carries a badge that says how many tasks it belongs to, and whether they are archived.

When nothing you have connected can list issues or pull requests, **Add issue** and **Add PR** in the **New task** composer open on a connect view, **Connect where your work lives**. Connect each provider you use, then click **Continue**. On the **Resources** screen, an empty list offers **Connect your code host** or **Connect your issue tracker** instead.

You can also start work on a pull request from GitLens or GitKraken Desktop. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).

### Create and manage GitHub pull requests

With GitHub connected, you can open and manage GitHub.com pull requests from Kepler.

To open a pull request, follow these steps:

1. Push your branch. Both branches must already exist in the repository.
2. Click **Create pull request** at the top right of the **Todo** list.
3. Choose the **Repository**, and type the **Head branch** and the **Base branch**.
4. Add a **Title** and a **Description**, and click **Create pull request**.

To change a pull request, click **Manage pull request**, the **…** button in the pull request's panel header. The dialog offers one button for each action GitHub allows you:

- **Edit title and description**
- **Close pull request**, or **Reopen pull request** on a closed one
- **Merge pull request**, which then asks for the **Merge method**. When the base branch uses a merge queue, **Add to merge queue** takes its place

---

---
# Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use Settings to change how Kepler, your agents, and your tasks work.

To open Settings, click the gear icon in the top bar, or press **Ctrl/⌘ + ,**. Settings opens over the page you are on. To close it, click **Close**, click outside it, or press **Escape**. The gear icon and **Ctrl/⌘ + ,** close it too.

To make Settings taller or shorter, drag its top or bottom edge. In the desktop app, **Open in new window** in its header moves Settings into a window of its own.

***

## The Settings pages

The Settings sidebar starts with a **Search settings** field and [**Setup**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#setup), a progress ring that reopens the first-run checklist. Below them, it lists these pages:

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [**Account**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#account) | Who you're signed in as, your organization, and GitKraken AI credits |
| [**Profiles**](/kepler/kepler-profiles) | The profiles on this computer, each with its own tasks, settings, and sign-ins. Desktop app only |
| [**Agents**](/kepler/settings-agents) | Your agents, the agent and mode new sessions start with, custom agents, agent presets, keeping agents running, and idle agents |
| [**Tasks**](/kepler/settings-tasks) | How new tasks start, where tasks open, how a task's page and Dashboard panels look, and task groups |
| [**Repositories**](/kepler/settings-repositories) | Where repositories and worktrees go and how branches are named, your repos and folders, worktrees and branches, and Projects |
| [**Integrations**](/kepler/settings-integrations) | Issue tracker and Git host connections |
| [**Actions**](/kepler/settings-actions) | Suggested Actions per item kind, and the Action list |
| [**Agent tools**](/kepler/settings-agent-tools) | MCP servers, and Kepler's built-in tools your agents can use |
| [**Approvals**](/kepler/settings-approvals) | The rules that approve your agents' actions for you |
| [**General**](/kepler/settings-app#general) | Language, the default editor, sessions started outside Kepler, and windows |
| [**Appearance**](/kepler/settings-app#appearance) | Light or dark appearance and themes, the Dashboard's views, the code font, and diff layout |
| [**Chat and terminal**](/kepler/settings-app#chat-and-terminal) | The chat's send key, width, and scrolling, and the terminal's font, message box, and links |
| [**Notifications**](/kepler/settings-app#notifications) | Which agent events notify you, on the desktop, in Kepler, and on a phone |
| [**Voice**](/kepler/settings-app#voice) | A check of your microphone and speaker, dictation with its models and vocabulary, and read aloud, all on this device |
| [**Keyboard shortcuts**](/kepler/settings-app#keyboard-shortcuts) | Kepler's keyboard shortcuts, and the keys you choose for them |
| [**Remote environments**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-environments) | The machines your agents can run on, over SSH or WSL |
| [**Remote Access**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-access) | Opening this Kepler from another device |
| [**Updates**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#updates) | The installed version, app updates, and agent updates |
| [**Help**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#help) | The docs, release notes, onboarding guides, and Kepler's logs |

The account menu also opens **Account**.

### Find a setting

To find a setting by name, start typing when Settings opens: **Search settings** already has focus. Results include single settings, and clicking one opens Settings at its control. Search also matches help text and common synonyms, so a word like *theme* or *notifications* finds the right setting. Type an agent's name to open its page.

When a search result or an Ask Kepler link takes you to a setting, Kepler highlights its control. If the setting is not shown, for example because it depends on something you have not set up yet, Kepler says why.

Ask Kepler can also search Kepler's settings, and change one when you ask. It names the setting as a link you can click. Some changes need your approval first. Settings that hold secrets, such as your account or integrations, can only be linked. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

To jump to a section, use the section links the Settings sidebar shows under the page you have open.

### Sub-pages and unsaved changes

When you open an item to edit it, such as a repository, a project, a custom agent, an MCP server, or an Action, it opens as a sub-page inside its Settings page, with a breadcrumb back to the page.

A sub-page form saves when you click **Save** in its footer. If a save fails, the footer shows why and keeps your edits on the form.

If you leave a sub-page with unsaved changes, however you leave, Kepler asks whether to save them before it discards anything.

Most fields outside those forms save themselves and show their status beside them. If a save fails, Kepler shows the reason, and names the setting if you have already left the page.

**Go back**, or your mouse's back button, closes Settings from any page or sub-page, and returns you to what you were doing before you opened it. To move between Settings pages, use the sidebar or a sub-page's breadcrumb.

### Settings in a remote window

In a window connected to a remote environment, Settings shows that machine's settings, and its header names the machine. Under its title, each page says where its settings are saved:

- **Saved on *machine***: on the remote machine.
- **Saved on this machine**: on your own computer, for every Kepler window on it.

A section that saves somewhere other than its page has its own badge. To change this machine's own settings from a remote window, click **Open this machine's settings** in the header. The same page opens in a local window.

Some settings are kept on your own computer, such as the language, the default editor, the themes, the terminal font, the code font, and the diff layout. If Ask Kepler in a remote window changes one of these, the change applies on your computer, and a notification names it, with **Undo**. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

---

---
# Setup and Account Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-setup-account/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Setup** to get back to Kepler's first-run checklist. Use **Account** to see who you are signed in as, which organization you are acting as, and how you are using your GitKraken AI credits. Use **Profiles** to keep separate sets of work on this computer.

## Setup

To reopen the first-run checklist, click **Setup** at the top of the Settings sidebar, under **Search settings**. Its progress ring shows how much of the checklist is done. For what the checklist asks you to do, and how to hide it from the toolbar, see [Getting Started → Finish the setup checklist](/kepler/kepler-getting-started#finish-the-setup-checklist).

***

## Account

The **Account** page has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Account** | Who you are signed in as, with your name and email |
| Organization | Your active organization and its plan. If your GitKraken account belongs to more than 1 organization, this line is a switcher |
| **Refresh account status** | Reads your plan again. Kepler also picks up a purchase or plan change you make outside the app by itself, without a restart |
| **Manage account** / **Manage subscription** | Opens your GitKraken account or subscription on gitkraken.dev |
| **GitKraken AI credits** | Your credit balance, with **Buy credits**, and **Your usage by feature**. Shown only when there is a balance to show |

The organization you are acting as decides what a feature costs.

**Your usage by feature** shows where your AI credits went. It appears once you have used an AI feature. A stacked bar splits your use between your 3 most-used AI features and everything else, shown as **Other**. Below the bar, each feature has a row with its share of your use as a percentage, such as **Commit Message**, **Conflict Resolution**, **Compose Changes**, or **Task & branch names**. To see what a feature does, hover its help icon.

***

## Profiles

**Profiles**, right under **Account** in the desktop app, lists the profiles on this computer. Each profile has its own tasks, repositories, settings, and sign-ins, and runs side by side with the others. Click **Add profile** to add one, or use a profile's row menu to edit, open, or delete it. When a remote machine you connect to has profiles from your other computers, they are listed under **On *machine***. From there, you can open one on this computer or remove it from the machine. See [Use Profiles in Kepler](/kepler/kepler-profiles).

---

---
# Use Profiles in Kepler
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/kepler-profiles/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

A profile in Kepler by GitKraken is a separate Kepler setup on the same computer. Each profile has its own tasks, repositories, folders, settings, and themes, and its own GitKraken sign-in and agent logins. Profiles run side by side, so you can keep work, personal, and client work apart and still have them all open at once.

## Requirements and limits

- Profiles are in the Kepler desktop app only.
- To add or open a profile, sign in to your GitKraken account.
- Every install starts with 1 profile, the default profile, named **Default**. It always stays first in the list, and you cannot delete it.

***

## Manage your profiles

To see and manage your profiles, open **Settings → Profiles**, right under **Account**. You can also choose **Manage profiles…** from the account menu. The list shows each profile with its color, and marks the one this window belongs to as **This profile**. Each row has a menu with **Edit**, **Open**, and **Delete…**.

### Profiles on your other machines

Each profile that connects to a [remote machine](/kepler/remote-environments) gets its own server there, and other computers can share it. When a machine you connect to already has profiles from another computer, **Settings → Profiles** lists them under **On *machine***. Each row's menu has these items:

- **Open on this computer** opens that profile here as a profile of its own, with the tasks your other computer made on that machine.
- **Remove from *machine*…** deletes the profile's server on that machine, with its tasks, conversations, and settings there, for every computer that uses it. Task folders on the machine stay.

To have one of your profiles use a profile on another machine instead, choose **Use a profile from another machine…** from its row menu. The profile reopens with that profile's tasks and sessions. Its local tasks and settings stay.

If a machine's server is signed in to a different GitKraken account than this computer, Kepler asks which account to keep when you connect. See [When the server uses another GitKraken account](/kepler/remote-environments#when-the-server-uses-another-gitkraken-account).

## Add a profile

1. In **Settings → Profiles**, click **Add profile**. You can also run **Add profile** from the command palette, or choose **Add profile…** from the account menu before you have a second profile.
2. Enter a **Name** and pick a **Profile color**.
3. Under **Start from**, choose one of these:
   - **Blank profile** starts like a clean install. You sign in and set it up the first time it opens.
   - **Copy of** a profile keeps that profile's settings, repositories, themes, and GitKraken sign-in. Its tasks and agent logins stay behind, and you can sign in to another GitKraken account after it opens.
4. Click **Add** to add the profile, or **Add and open** to also open it in a new window.

If a machine you connect to already has profiles from another computer, the dialog lists them too, so you can open one here instead of adding a new profile.

Each agent keeps a separate sign-in in each profile, unless its page in **Settings → Agents** says it uses your own sign-in in every profile. Signing in or out of such an agent changes it everywhere.

## Switch between profiles

Each profile opens in its own windows. To open another profile, or bring its windows forward, use one of these:

- The account menu in the top bar shows this window's profile, marked **This window**. Under **Other profiles**, click a profile to open it. Profiles from your other computers are listed under **On *machine***.
- The tray icon's menu lists each profile with its windows and **New Window**. A profile that is running shows **(Running)** after its name.
- The command palette has **Open profile:** and the name of each profile.
- In **Settings → Profiles**, choose **Open** from a profile's row menu.

Once you have more than 1 profile, each window's title names its profile.

## Rename, recolor, or reorder a profile

To rename a profile or change its color, choose **Edit** from its row menu. To color the top of every window in that profile, turn on **Tint this profile's windows**. A window connected to a remote machine shows that machine's color instead.

To reorder your profiles, drag a row by its handle, use **Move profile up** and **Move profile down** in its menu, or press **Alt/⌥ + ↑** or **Alt/⌥ + ↓**.

## Quit with several profiles open

While another profile is running, the tray's **Quit** reads **Quit All**, and each other profile has its own **Quit *profile*** item. Quitting the default profile quits every profile. Kepler asks once, and any profile with agent sessions still working asks before it quits. When Kepler installs an update, it closes and reopens every profile that was running.

## Delete a profile

1. Quit the profile if it is running.
2. In **Settings → Profiles**, choose **Delete…** from its row menu.
3. To also delete the profile's folder in your home folder, select **Also delete its folder**. That folder holds the repositories the profile cloned, its worktrees, and its task folders. Work there may exist nowhere else and cannot be recovered.
4. Click **Delete *profile*** to confirm.

Deleting a profile removes its tasks, conversations, settings, and repository list from this computer, and signs it out of GitKraken and its agents. Its servers on remote machines stay, with their tasks, so other computers using the profile keep working. To remove one, use **Remove from *machine*…** in [Profiles on your other machines](#profiles-on-your-other-machines). Your accounts, your other profiles, and repositories added from elsewhere are not affected.

***

---

---
# Agent Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-agents/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Settings → Agents** to choose how new sessions start, to install, update, and sign in to the coding agents that work on your tasks, to add custom agents and agent presets, to keep agents running, and to put idle agents to sleep. Your agents' MCP servers and built-in tools are on [Agent tools](/kepler/settings-agent-tools), and the rules that approve their actions for you are on [Approvals](/kepler/settings-approvals).

<a id="default-agent"></a>

## Defaults

**Defaults** sets how new sessions and Ask Kepler chats start:

| Setting | What it controls |
|---|---|
| **New sessions start with** | The agent that the **New task** composer, the Dashboard's composer, and a new draft session start with |
| **New Ask Kepler chats start with** | The agent that new [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler) chats start with |
| **New sessions start in** | Whether new sessions run in **Chat** or **Terminal**, for every agent. See [Default mode for new sessions](#default-mode-for-new-sessions) |

**New sessions start with** and **New Ask Kepler chats start with** are agent-settings pills, like the one in the composer: pick the agent and account, and optionally an [agent preset](#agent-presets), a model, and other options. Kepler saves each pick as you make it. An [Action](/kepler/actions) uses **New sessions start with** unless it names an agent of its own.

Below each pill, **Start each session on the agent you used last** and **Start each chat on the agent you used last** are on by default. Your first session or chat uses the pill's agent, and each later one starts on your last pick. To always start on the pill's agent, clear the box.

**New Ask Kepler chats start with** lists only the agents that run in **Chat**, because only they can answer in the Ask Kepler panel. See [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler#which-agents-can-answer).

### Default mode for new sessions

**New sessions start in** chooses where new sessions run. **Chat** runs your agents inside Kepler, and **Terminal** runs each agent's own command-line app. The default is **Chat**.

This setting applies to every agent that can run in both modes, including agents you add later. To give one agent its own mode, open the agent from [Your agents](#your-agents) and set **New sessions start in** on its page. Choosing a mode under **Defaults** again sets it for every agent.

The setting is only a default: you can pick the other mode when you start a session. A terminal-only agent always starts in Terminal. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

## Your agents

Kepler supports **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Pi**, **Auggie**, **Antigravity**, **Cursor**, and **Grok Build**. Settings lists the agents installed on this machine first.

In the section header, **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater, and **Rescan** looks again for the agent CLIs installed on this machine. If you install or remove an agent outside Kepler, click **Rescan**.

Each agent has a row with its version, a **Default** badge on your default agent, and its accounts or sign-in state. A row also has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Install** | Opens **Set up *agent*** to pick an install method, then **Sign in to *agent*** if the agent needs a sign-in. Shown when the agent is not installed and has an installer for your OS |
| **Add account** | Opens the agent's page and its add-account dialog |
| **Sign in** | Signs in to an agent that has a single login |
| The on/off switch | Off keeps the agent installed but hides it when you start work |

If you installed the agent yourself, use **Already installed?** in the **Set up *agent*** dialog: enter or browse to the program, then click **Use this**.

When a newer version of an installed agent is out, its row shows **Update available**. After an update, the row shows **Updated**: new sessions use the new version, and a running session switches when you restart it. To turn off the title-bar notice and the restart notice for agent updates, see [Settings → Updates](/kepler/settings-updates-help#updates).

When Kepler runs the copy of an agent that came with its vendor's desktop app, the agent shows a **Desktop app** badge. That copy updates only when you update the app. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations#install-an-agent).

When the version reads **Version unknown**, Kepler turns off features that depend on the version, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. To fix it, reinstall or update the agent.

### An agent's own page

To open an agent's page, click its row. The page holds the agent's own settings:

| Setting | What it controls |
|---|---|
| **New sessions start in** | This agent's own mode, instead of the [default for every agent](#default-mode-for-new-sessions) |
| **Update** | Runs the agent's updater and shows its output. Shown when Kepler has an updater for that agent |
| **Install CLI** | Shown when Kepler runs a desktop app's copy of the agent. Installs the standalone CLI, which updates itself, and Kepler runs it instead |
| The switch beside **Update** | On by default. Off keeps the agent installed but hides it when you start work |
| **Accounts** | Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build: runs more than 1 login side by side. See [Use several accounts for one agent](#use-several-accounts-for-one-agent) |
| **Account** | On an agent with a single login: who is signed in, with **Sign in** or **Sign out**. Signing out deletes the stored credentials |
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Which *agent* Kepler runs** | The agent program Kepler runs. **Auto** uses the first match on your `PATH`, the same one `which` finds. To override it, pick a specific install or **Custom path…**, or click **Rescan** to search again |
| **Where *agent* keeps its data** | Set it only to keep the copy Kepler runs apart from the one you run yourself. Empty uses the agent's usual folder |

If the installed version of an agent has a known problem, a warning note on its page says what to do:

| Note | What it means |
|---|---|
| OpenCode *version* is not supported | Sessions with this version do not start. Install OpenCode 2, or choose an OpenCode 2 program under **Which OpenCode Kepler runs** |
| Auggie integration is unverified | Kepler could not verify the selected Auggie build. Before you rely on MCP tools in Chat, click **Rescan** or select a verified installation under **Which Auggie Kepler runs** |
| Codex *version* can show approval prompts that need no answer | Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

**OpenCode needs version 2.** If you have both versions installed, point **Which OpenCode Kepler runs** at OpenCode 2. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes in OpenCode 2.

**Google Antigravity runs the `agy` CLI in both modes.** Chat needs Antigravity CLI 1.5.0 or newer. With an older CLI, click **Update** on its page. Chat and Terminal share one sign-in: **Sign in in Terminal**. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations#sign-in-to-an-agent).

### Use several accounts for one agent

With **Accounts**, you can run more than 1 login for an agent side by side. Each account has its own credentials and history, but shares your skills, agents, commands, and settings.

To add an account, click **Add account**, on the agent's row or its page. For Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot, also choose whether its conversations **Keep separate** or **Share with the CLI**. A new Copilot account starts on **Share with the CLI**, and its new conversations use your CLI settings. If you change a Copilot account's choice later, the conversations it already has stay where they are and still open in Kepler.

Each account row has the following controls:

- A color picker that tints the agent icon wherever that account runs. The default account starts with **No color**.
- **Sign in**.
- An account menu with **Rename**, **Share history with the CLI**, **Sign in another way**, **Sign out**, and **Remove account**. On a signed-in Claude Code account, the menu also has **Switch account…**, which signs that account in with a different Claude login. See [Switch the account a Claude Code login uses](#switch-the-account-a-claude-code-login-uses).

Once an agent has 2 or more accounts, Kepler uses them in list order, top first:

- A new session you start without picking an account starts on the first account with usage left.
- When a session hits a usage limit, Kepler continues it on the first account with usage left, or suggests that account, depending on [When a usage limit is reached](#keep-agents-running).

To reorder the list, drag a row by its handle, or use **Move to top**, **Move up**, and **Move down** in the account menu. To keep an account out of the switch at a usage limit, clear **Use at a usage limit** in its menu. Its row then reads **Skipped at a usage limit**. An account that keeps its own history reads **New sessions only**, because a conversation can move to it only with **Share history with the CLI** on.

Removing an account stops its running sessions and deletes the sessions stored only in that account. To keep those sessions, click **Move to CLI account** first. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#several-accounts-for-one-agent).

### When an added account stops sharing your settings

An added account shares your own settings, instructions, skills, agents, commands, and other configuration. If the agent saves a change while signed in to that account, it can write its own copy, and the account stops following your file. Kepler then shows a message under the account's row. Expand it to see both files, and choose one of the following:

- **Ask Kepler to resolve** opens an Ask Kepler chat with a prompt you can edit, asking the agent to copy what is worth keeping into your shared copy.
- **Share your *item* again** links the account back to your file, and saves its own copy as a backup next to it.
- **Keep its own *item*** keeps the account's copy. You can still choose **Share your *item* again** later from the row's menu.

### Switch the account a Claude Code login uses

**Switch account…** opens a dialog that names the login now signed in, and how many running sessions use the account. Running sessions pick up the new login when they restart or on their next request. On the default account, the one the CLI uses, the switch also changes the account the `claude` command uses in your own terminals.

Click **Continue** to open the usual sign-in. If your browser is already signed in, choose a different account on the sign-in page.

### Artifacts in new sessions

The following setting is on Claude Code's page:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Gives new sessions the Artifact tools, which publish pages and designs and add about 12k tokens to each session's context | Off |

A running Chat session has its own **Artifacts** switch in its agent settings. When you turn it on, Kepler asks first, then restarts the session and resumes the conversation. Once a conversation has artifacts on, they stay on for that conversation. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

### Let artifact comments start turns

The following setting is on Claude Code's page:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Lets anyone with edit access to an artifact a Chat session publishes start a turn in that session by sending a comment to Claude | On |

Running sessions keep the value they started with. When you change the setting, the page lists the sessions still on the previous value. To apply the new value, click **Restart all**, or tick sessions and click **Restart selected**.

Restarting keeps each conversation. It interrupts a turn in progress and stops background work, and a restarted session stops watching the artifacts it published before.

## Custom agents

To run an agent that Kepler does not list, add it as a custom agent by giving Kepler its command. To add one, click **New custom agent** in the section header. To edit one, click its row. Either way, the agent opens as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name Kepler shows for the agent |
| **Command** | The program to run, for example `/usr/local/bin/my-agent` or `my-agent` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments passed to the command |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Environment for the command |
| **Runs in** | **Chat**, Kepler's chat, for a program that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). **Terminal**, the command's own app in a terminal |

Custom agents appear with the built-in agents wherever you pick an agent.

Kepler encrypts environment values at rest and hides existing values when you edit an agent. To keep a stored secret, leave its value empty (`KEY=`). To replace it, type a new value.

**Delete** asks first, then deletes the agent and the environment values stored with it. You cannot undo a delete.

## Agent presets

An agent preset saves one agent's model, mode, and other options, such as effort, under a name, so you can pick them all at once whenever you pick that agent. The list groups your presets by agent, with the agent's badge beside each name:

- To add a preset, click **New preset** in the section header, or click **Save preset** in a session's agent settings.
- To edit a preset, click its row.
- To duplicate, reorder, or delete a preset, use its menu.

A preset opens as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | A name no other preset uses |
| **Agent** | The agent the preset belongs to, with its **Model**, **Mode**, and other options |
| **MCP servers** | Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot: **On** or **Off** for each of the agent's MCP servers, with **Reset** |

A preset's MCP server choices apply to each session that uses it. A server that is off in the agent's own settings can only stay off. **Save preset** in a session's agent settings keeps the MCP servers you switched for that session. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers#per-session).

You can use a preset in these places:

- **A session's agent settings.** In the composer, pick it in the **Preset** row, which appears when the chosen agent has presets. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#agent-model-mode-and-effort).
- **The default agents.** The **New sessions start with** and **New Ask Kepler chats start with** pills in [Defaults](#defaults).
- **Actions.** Each Action's **Preset** list, in the Action's editor. See [Actions](/kepler/actions).
- **Automations.** An automation's agent settings can use a preset. See [Automations](/kepler/kepler-automations).

If Actions or automations use a preset you delete, Kepler lists them and asks you to choose a replacement. If you change a preset that automations use, Kepler names them and asks you to confirm, and they use the updated options from their next run.

When you change a preset, running sessions that use it keep the earlier version until you update them. To apply the change, click **Update all** below the list. Updating keeps each conversation, but a session that needs a restart interrupts any turn in progress.

<a id="usage-limits"></a>
<a id="usage-and-recovery"></a>

## Keep agents running

**Keep agents running** keeps your agents working when the machine would sleep or Kepler quits, and when an agent hits a usage limit or its model is overloaded. **Keep agents running** and [Idle agents](#idle-agents) apply to the machine the agents run on, so in a window connected to a remote machine, they apply to that machine.

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep this machine awake while agents work** | Blocks sleep while an agent session is starting, running, or waiting for your input, and while Remote Access is on | On |
| **Keep agents and terminals running after Kepler quits or restarts** | Agents and terminals keep running while Kepler is closed or updating, and reconnect afterwards. When it is off, quitting or restarting Kepler ends them | On |
| **When a usage limit is reached** | What happens to a session that a usage limit cuts off, for every agent, in Chat and in Terminal. See the options below | Wait for the reset |
| **Retry automatically when the model is overloaded** | When the model is overloaded or the provider has a temporary server error, Kepler waits and asks the agent to continue, for up to 12 hours. It never resends your prompt | On |

**Keep this machine awake while agents work** also counts Claude Code sessions running outside Kepler. The screen can still turn off. If Kepler cannot keep the machine awake, the setting says why under it.

**Keep agents and terminals running after Kepler quits or restarts** applies from the next session you start. If agents and terminals cannot start on this machine, the setting says why.

**When a usage limit is reached** has these options:

- **Ask me**: the session stops, and its usage bar offers to switch accounts or wait for the reset.
- **Wait for the reset**: the session continues when the limit resets.
- **Switch accounts**: the session continues on the agent's next account with usage left, in [the order on its page](#use-several-accounts-for-one-agent), or after the reset if no account has any.

Kepler reads each account's plan usage from its provider, through the agent's own sign-in, and never changes that sign-in. If an account row on an agent's page shows **Turn on usage checks**, click it to turn those checks back on.

## Idle agents

**Idle agents** stops sessions you have left alone, once you are not looking at them:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Put idle task agents to sleep** | How long an agent in a task can stay quiet before Kepler stops it, from **After 5 minutes** to **After 24 hours**, or **Never** | After 1 hour |
| **Put idle Ask Kepler chats to sleep** | How long an Ask Kepler chat can stay quiet before Kepler stops it | After 15 minutes |
| **Wake idle terminal agents to read new reports** | Types a one-line note into a sleeping terminal agent's empty input when a report reaches it | On |

A sleeping session's status reads **Asleep**. Your next message wakes it, and the conversation carries on. Agents in a terminal sleep too, once nothing is typed into them and nothing they started is still running. Typing into the terminal wakes them. Agents that are working or waiting on you stay awake. See [Session status](/kepler/agent-sessions#session-status).

## Agent tools

MCP servers and Kepler's [built-in tools](/kepler/settings-agent-tools#built-in-tools) are on **Settings → Agent tools**: see [Agent Tool Settings](/kepler/settings-agent-tools).

### MCP servers

**MCP servers** is a section of **Settings → Agent tools**: see [MCP servers](/kepler/settings-agent-tools#mcp-servers).

## Approvals

The rules that approve your agents' actions for you are on **Settings → Approvals**: see [Approval Settings](/kepler/settings-approvals).

***

---

---
# Task Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-tasks/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Settings → Tasks** to choose how new tasks start, where tasks open, and how a task's page and Dashboard panels look, and to manage your task groups. A task is one piece of work: its prompt, the agent sessions working on it, and the worktree or folder they work in.

## New tasks

**New tasks** sets what Kepler preselects for every new task: where the task makes changes, where its files go, and whether Kepler names the task for you. These values belong to the environment you are working on, so in a remote window they are the remote machine's.

### Default agent

**New tasks** shows the agent new sessions start with. To change it, click **Change in Agents**, which opens [Defaults](/kepler/settings-agents#defaults) in **Settings → Agents**. There you also choose the agent Ask Kepler chats start with, and whether new sessions start in **Chat** or **Terminal**. An [Action](/kepler/actions) uses the default agent unless it names an agent of its own.

### Where new tasks make changes

**Where new tasks make changes** sets what a repository starts on when you attach it to a new task in the **New task** composer. Pick one of these options from its dropdown:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Isolated worktree** | The default. Creates a new branch in its own worktree, so agents can work in parallel |
| **New branch** | Creates a new branch in the repository's own checkout, with no worktree |
| **Current branch** | Works on whichever branch the repository's own checkout has |

This setting is only the default. For a single task, the repository chip's own **Base branch** and **Isolated worktree** controls override it. Under **Isolated worktree**, the composer names the default as **New tasks:** and the option, and **Change** opens this setting. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#configuring-a-repository).

**With New branch and Current branch, commits land on whichever branch is checked out at the time**, because both work in the repository's own checkout. If another task is already working in that checkout, Kepler says so and offers to switch that repository to an isolated worktree instead.

New branches start with the branch prefix, and new worktrees go in the worktrees folder, whichever option you choose. **New tasks** shows both, and **Change in Repositories** opens them in [Settings → Repositories → Default locations](/kepler/settings-repositories#default-locations).

### Folder locations

The following setting decides where each task keeps its files:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Tasks folder** | *Each task gets a folder here for its attachments and files.* | `~/kepler/tasks` |

Type a path, or click **Choose a folder** beside the field to browse. An edit saves when you leave the field. The worktrees folder and the repositories folder are in [Settings → Repositories](/kepler/settings-repositories#default-locations).

### Automatically name new tasks

The following setting names new tasks for you:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Automatically name new tasks** | *Names a new task with AI from its prompt and attached resources. A task created from a single issue or PR keeps that item's name.* | On |

A change takes effect on the next task you create.

<a id="task-page"></a>

## Task page and panels

**Task page and panels** sets where a task opens and how its page and Dashboard panel look. Kepler saves these settings on this machine:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Where tasks open** | Whether a task you open from a link, Go To, or a notification opens as its own page or as a Dashboard panel | Automatic |
| **Where a new task opens on the Dashboard** | Where a new task's panel appears among the open panels | Beside the focused panel |
| **Show tabs on the task page** | Keeps sessions, worktrees, and resources open as tabs you can pin, drag between groups, and arrange side by side | Off |
| **Preview tabs** | *A single click opens a preview that the next click replaces. Double-click, or edit, to keep it open.* | On |
| **Open the side pane in Dashboard panels** | When a Dashboard panel has room, shows its worktree's changes beside the session, or its resources when it has no worktree | Only when there are changes |

**Where tasks open** has these options:

- **Automatic** opens a Dashboard panel when you are on the Dashboard, and the task page everywhere else.
- **Task page** always opens the task's own page.
- **Dashboard panel** always opens a Dashboard panel.

The phone app always opens the task page.

With **Show tabs on the task page** off, each column of a task shows one thing at a time, and you switch between them from the list on the left. **Preview tabs** works only with it turned on. Sessions always open as permanent tabs. See [The task view](/kepler/task-view).

**Open the side pane in Dashboard panels** has these options:

- **Always** opens the side pane whenever the panel has room.
- **Only when there are changes** opens it for a worktree with uncommitted files or commits on its branch.
- **Never** leaves it closed. Open it from the panel header.

Closing the pane keeps it closed for that task in that view.

### Where a new task opens on the Dashboard

**Where a new task opens on the Dashboard** sets where the panel of a task you start, or open from a notification, appears among the Dashboard's open panels. Pick one of these options from its dropdown:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Beside the focused panel** | The default. Opens the panel next to the one you are reading, or at the end once the panels fill more than one row |
| **At the end** | Always opens the panel after every open panel |

## Groups

**Groups** lists all your task groups, including archived ones. To open it from the Dashboard, choose **Manage groups…** in a group header's menu.

- To add a group, click **New group** in the section header.
- To edit a group's name or color, click its name.
- To reorder groups, drag a row by its grip.
- To archive or delete a group, use its **⋮** menu. You can archive a group once all its tasks are archived.

Archived groups are listed under **Archived**, where their menu has **Restore group**. When you delete a group, its tasks stay, ungrouped, unless you tick **Also delete its {count} tasks** in the confirmation. See [Your groups](/kepler/arranging-your-work#your-groups).

***

---

---
# Repository Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-repositories/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-11

Use **Settings → Repositories** to set where Kepler clones repositories and creates worktrees, and how it names branches. Here you also add, trust, and edit the repositories and folders Kepler tracks, clean up worktrees and branches, and group repositories into projects.

<a id="repositories-folder"></a>

## Default locations

**Default locations** sets where Kepler puts repositories and worktrees, and how it names the branches it creates:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Repositories folder** | Where Kepler clones repositories, and where it looks for repositories to add | `~/kepler/repositories` |
| **Worktrees folder** | *Where Kepler creates worktrees, for new tasks and when an agent asks for one.* | `~/kepler/worktrees` |
| **Branch prefix** | *Starts the name of every branch Kepler creates. A repo can set its own in its settings.* | `kepler/` |

Type a path, or click **Choose a folder** beside a folder field to browse. An edit saves when you leave the field. If the **Repositories folder** does not exist yet, Kepler creates it when you clone.

### Scan the repositories folder

To add every repository already in the repositories folder, click **Scan for repositories** beside the field. Kepler scans only when you change the setting or click the button. A scan skips any repository you removed; to bring one back, add it yourself with **Add repo**. Repositories a scan adds start untrusted, and the message after the scan offers to trust them, or to trust the folder they are in. See [Trust a repository](#trust-a-repository).

After a scan that added repositories, **Undo** removes them again, except any you have used or changed since the scan. To scan, the setting needs a full folder path before any variable in it.

To trust every repository in this folder, including ones added there later, tick **Trust everything in this folder** under the field.

### Worktrees folder

If a **Worktrees folder** has text before `<REPOSITORY_PATH>`, Kepler adds each repository's full path after that text. The field suggests 2 patterns that work: worktrees next to each repository, or a subfolder per repository. On Windows, Kepler does not save a path like this, so use one of the 2 patterns.

### Branch prefix

The prefix applies to **automatic** names only. Kepler uses a branch name you type exactly as you typed it, so a repository with an enforced `feat/` or `fix/` push rule still works. If your prefix does not end in a separator, Kepler adds a `/`, so `team` becomes `team/`, while `ea-` stays as you typed it.

To override the prefix for one repository, use its [Edit repo](#edit-a-repository) page.

### The Variables menu

A folder field that takes variables has a **Variables** menu beside it. Pick a variable, such as **REPOSITORY PATH**, to insert it at the cursor. Kepler fills it in when it creates the folder, so one pattern works for every repository. Each field offers only the variables it can fill in:

| Field | Variables offered |
|---|---|
| **Worktrees folder** | `<REPOSITORY_PATH>` (*Main repo folder*), `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` (*Repo name*) |
| **Repositories folder** | `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` |

For example, `<REPOSITORY_PATH>/.worktrees/<REPOSITORY_NAME>` nests each worktree inside the repository it belongs to.

Per-repository commands have a **Variables** menu of their own, with 2 more variables. See [Per-repository commands](#per-repository-commands).

## Your repos and folders

**Your repos and folders** lists every repository Kepler tracks and every folder you have attached to a task. Each row shows its name, its path on disk, how many commands it has, and a shield that shows whether you trust it. The section has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Filter repos and folders** | Narrows the list by name |
| **Show** | Lists **All**, **Trusted**, or **Untrusted** repos and folders, each with a count |
| Shield | Trusts the row, or stops trusting it, in one click |
| A row | Click it to open the repository's **Edit repo** page, or the folder's page |
| **Add repo** | Opens the **Add repo** page. See below |
| **Add folder…** | Adds a plain folder |
| Trash icon | Stops tracking the repository or folder, and leaves the folder on disk |

If a folder you added later becomes a Git repository, for example after `git init`, Kepler treats it as a repository from then on.

Removing a repository deletes its sessions, terminals, and configured commands, and ends any live agent and terminal sessions tied to it. Kepler asks you to confirm first.

### Add a repository

To add a repository, follow these steps:

1. Click **Add repo**.
2. In **Folder or URL**, paste a URL to clone, or pick a folder that already holds a repository. You can also drop a folder onto the page, or click **Create a new repo instead**.
3. Kepler shows what it found as a card, and says what it will do, such as clone into a new folder or add an existing clone as it is. It also tells you when the repository is already in Kepler, or the folder is not a Git repository. Edit the name, description, and branch prefix on the card if you need to.
4. Click **Add repo**, or **Clone** for a URL.

You can leave the page while a clone runs; the clone continues, and a notification tells you when it finishes or why it failed.

### Edit a repository

Click a repository's row to open its **Edit repo** page. The page shows the repository's path, its remote, and its branches. When Kepler knows the remote's host, click the remote's provider line to open the repository there (**Open on {provider}**). The page has these parts:

| Part | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Name** | How this repo is listed in Kepler. Leave it empty to use the folder name |
| **Aliases** | Short names for this repo when talking to agents, separated by commas, such as `api, backend` |
| **Description** | What this repo is for. Agents working in it read this |
| **Trusted** | A checkbox that lets Kepler run git in this repo. See [Trust a repository](#trust-a-repository) |
| **Branch prefix** | Overrides the prefix from [Default locations](#default-locations) for this repository only. See below |
| **Branch synchronization** | How this repo's branches update by default (**Rebase** or **Merge**), and whether to push after an update. See [Update worktrees](#update-worktrees) |
| **Commands** | Shell commands for this repository. See [Per-repository commands](#per-repository-commands) |
| **MCP servers** | Extra tools your agents get in this repo, on top of their own lists. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers) |

**Name**, **Aliases**, and **Description** are optional. The page has no **Save** button: each field saves on its own and shows its save status. Some fields have more rules:

- A repository you name keeps that name exactly.
- An alias cannot contain a colon, or repeat another repository's alias or name.
- Agents working in this repo read the description, so write a full sentence.

In a WSL window, a repository stored on a Windows drive shows a warning on its Edit repo page, because git and agents are slow from WSL there. For faster access, clone it into the Linux file system, such as your home folder.

#### Branch prefix, per repository

The **Branch prefix** control has 3 options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Default ({value})** | Uses the prefix from [Default locations](#default-locations) |
| **None** | Creates task branches with no prefix |
| **Custom** | A prefix for this repository only |

**New task branches will look like** shows an example branch name for your choice.

Kepler does not save a prefix that the repository already uses as a local branch name. Rename that branch, or choose another prefix.

#### Trust a repository

Kepler runs no git in a repository or folder you have not trusted, because a repository's own settings can run programs. Until you trust it, its status, branches, and changes stay empty.

To trust a repository or folder, use one of these:

- Click the shield on its row in **Your repos and folders**, or tick **Trusted** on its page. If a trusted folder covers the repository, **Trusted** is ticked and dimmed, and its help names the folder to change it in.
- At the top of **Your repos and folders**, under **Trusted folders**, click **Trust a folder…** to trust everything inside a folder, including what you add there later. You cannot trust a whole drive or filesystem root. A repository trusted this way shows **via** and the folder. To stop trusting it, remove the folder from **Trusted folders**.
- Under **Show**, pick **Untrusted** to see untrusted repos and folders grouped by parent folder. Tick rows and trust them together from the bar at the bottom, or trust a group's whole folder with the **Trust** button beside it.
- Click **Trust**, **Trust and retry**, or **Trust and start** where Kepler asks, such as in a task's Changes view or when you start a task in the **New task** composer.

While a repository is trusted, agent sessions in it also skip the agent's own trust question.

### Per-repository commands

Use commands to run your dev server, tests, or build from a task's worktree in one click. A command can also run when Kepler creates a new worktree, for example to install dependencies. Commands are shell commands for one repository. An agent can also add, change, or delete a repository's commands, and asks for your approval first.

To add a command, click **Add command** in the **Commands** section of the Edit repo page. Each command row has these fields:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| Name | A label, for example *Install deps*. You pick the command by this name from the **Run** menu |
| Command | The shell command, for example `pnpm install`. Its **Variables** menu inserts any of the variables below |
| **Run on worktree creation** | Runs the command each time Kepler creates a worktree for this repository. Off by default |
| **Agents can start this without asking** | Lets an agent start this command from its task without asking you first |

To save a row, click **Add command** (or **Save** on a stored command), or press **Ctrl/⌘ + Enter**. Each command saves on its own.

Commands accept 4 variables, which Kepler fills in when the command runs:

| Variable | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `<REPOSITORY_PATH>` | Main repo folder |
| `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` | Repo name |
| `<SOURCE_PATH>` | Where files come from (the main repo, or the source worktree when forking) |
| `<WORKTREE_PATH>` | The new worktree folder |

To reorder commands, drag a row by its handle, or move it from the keyboard with **Alt/⌥ + ↑** and **Alt/⌥ + ↓**. A new order saves at once. The order sets the order of the **Run** menu, and the order in which commands set to run on worktree creation run.

A row needs both a name and a command before you can save it. A closed row that is not saved yet shows **Not saved**. **Remove command** deletes a saved command, and the notification that follows offers **Undo**.

Commands set to run on worktree creation run one at a time, in list order. If one fails, Kepler skips the rest. Each command runs in the new worktree's folder. On macOS and Linux, it runs through your login shell, so tools set up in your shell profile, such as `nvm`, are available. On Windows, it runs in Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`). Each command has a 10-minute timeout.

A failed command does not undo the worktree. The worktree exists but may not be usable. To fix it:

1. Read the command output in the task.
2. Correct the command here.
3. Run it again from the **Run** menu.

An agent can start a stored command in a terminal on its own task, but never a command you have not stored. It asks you first if the repository is not trusted or **Agents can start this without asking** is cleared. **Always allow** on its request ticks that box. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

To run a command from the task view, right-click a worktree row in the task's context panel and use **Run command here**. It lists that repository's commands and runs the one you pick in that worktree, in a terminal. For a repository with no commands yet, **Create command…** opens the Edit repo page. To stop a running command, use the run button or its menu.

### Copy ignored files into new worktrees

A new worktree starts without your repository's git-ignored files, such as `.env`. To copy some of them, list them in a `.worktreeinclude` file at the repository's root, in the same format as `.gitignore`. Kepler copies them before any command set to run on worktree creation starts. It copies only files that git also ignores in the new worktree, so a copied secret cannot be committed by mistake, and it never overwrites a file already there.

## Worktrees and branches

To update, clean up, or delete worktrees and local branches across your repositories, click **Manage worktrees and branches** on the Repositories page. The **Worktrees and branches** sub-page opens.

On the sub-page, you can see which worktrees and local branches are stale, update the ones that are behind, and delete what is done. It lists every worktree, and every local branch that no worktree holds, grouped by repository, and a summary says how many look safe to delete. Kepler deletes nothing until you ask, and never deletes the base branch, which has a **Base** badge.

The sub-page has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Search branch, path or repo** | Narrows the list. Every word you type must match the branch, the path, or the repository name |
| **Show worktrees and branches** | Filters by status: **Safe to delete**, **Needs update**, **Conflicts**, **Stale**, or **All** |
| **Show worktrees, branches or both** | Shows **All**, **Worktrees only**, or **Branches only** |
| **Stale after** *n* **days** | Sets how many days without activity make a row stale. Defaults to 14 |
| **Re-check** | Fetches every repository's remotes and checks the list again |
| **Select all** | Selects the rows in the current view |
| Selection bar | Has **Clear**, **Create task**, **Update**, and **Delete**. **Update** and **Delete** act only on selected rows you can see |

**Create task** opens the **New task** composer with the selected worktrees and branches already added: each worktree as it is, and each branch without a worktree as a branch to work on. Kepler creates nothing until you start or prepare the task. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).

Each row shows the following:

- Where it stands with its upstream: commits to push (↑) and pull (↓), **No upstream**, or **Upstream gone**.
- How it compares with its base, such as **3 behind main**, and how many files are uncommitted.
- How long since it was last touched, and why it may be finished, such as being merged into its base.
- The tasks, sessions, and pull request tied to it. An **External** count shows sessions started outside Kepler.

With a Jira or Jira Server account connected, a row whose branch name references a Jira issue shows a chip for that issue. To open the issue in your browser, click the chip. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

A row counts as one or more of the following:

- **Safe to delete**: its work has landed (merged into the base, or its pull request merged or closed with the upstream gone), and nothing is uncommitted, unpushed, or in use.
- **Needs update**: behind the base branch with no known conflict, so an update can bring it up to date.
- **Conflicts**: behind the base branch, and merging the base in would conflict, so you have to update it by hand.
- **Stale**: no activity for longer than the stale threshold, but nothing proves the work landed. Deleting it can lose uncommitted or unpushed work.

**Needs update** and **Conflicts** leave out rows that are safe to delete.

### Delete worktrees and branches

Select rows, then click **Delete**. The confirmation says what is lost:

- For worktrees, their folders are removed from disk with anything the dialog lists. **Also delete the branches** deletes each worktree's branch too.
- For local branches, commits that exist only on them are lost. The dialog marks each branch that is not merged as **not merged**. **Force delete branches that are not merged** deletes those too, and **Also delete the branches on the remote** deletes the remote branches.

Kepler keeps any branch it cannot delete safely and says why, for example when a worktree still has it checked out. A local branch with commits that are not merged is kept too, and the result offers **Force delete** for it, which deletes the branch with those commits.

Kepler never deletes a repository's main checkout. It keeps any worktree that still has uncommitted or unpushed work, other tasks, running agent sessions, or a lock from another tool, and says why for each one.
